title: Love story: Supporting your soulmate through voluntary assisted dying
text:
Hilda Quiroga says she was "struck" by Steve Mayer from the moment they first met in Naarm/Melbourne in 2007. Hilda, who works in social services, and Steve, a barista and musician, went on to have an 18-year partnership and travel the world together, until his death at 53 through voluntary assisted dying (VAD).

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

The funny thing is I met him at a gym.

I hate gyms. He hated gyms with a passion.

But, he was the barista at a cafe in the gym and I was there signing up a client.

I noticed how kind and respectful he was towards her.

I knew nothing about him. He could have been married or gay for all I knew. But, I emailed my friend and said to him, "I have just met a man that is going to change my life."

Not long after I was off overseas by myself, but I took him with me in my mind. I wanted to tell him that day, "We're going to be travelling together mate, so get ready, get your passport ready."

We got together in February 2008 and three months later we moved in.

I was in my 30s. He was in his 30s. There's no point in wasting time.

I had been married before, but it was short. Steve just made me feel like he saw me.

I was 100 per cent sure that I'd met my soulmate. I cringe at that word, but I just knew, and we were together, inseparable from that day to the very last.

An 'unstoppable force'

He knew all about the places that I'd been to and all the places that I wanted to go — like all the Inca ruins — because he was so well read.

He'd never had the opportunity to travel, but then when we got together, we were like this unstoppable force.

He got his passport and found his travelling legs and because we had no children, we were free to just travel, work, travel. That was us.

He wanted to go to see Machu Picchu and the Amazon and take ayahuasca and we did.

Hilda Quiroga says the couple had "incredible adventures", which included travelling to Samoa, Guatemala and Peru. (Supplied: Hilda Quiroga)

A diagnosis

Everything changed in June 2023.

He had the results of a CT scan come back and they found a mass in his lung.

His only symptoms were that he was fatigued — which was not like Steve, who normally had the energy of a kid — and he was also sweating a lot.

A couple of days later tumours were found in his brain and elsewhere. It had already metastasised.

In September I quit my job. I had taken time off in those first months but was going to back work a little bit and it didn't feel right.

I successfully applied for carer's allowance and disability support.

It was tricky, but I'm good at paperwork.

In our relationship, Steve usually took care of cooking and cleaning (mostly because I'm not great), and I took care of social engagements, finances, and personal administration.

He taught me a lot about myself, and I didn't think I could do the things that I did when he got sick.

You're a partner, but you also become a "carer".

I've never been comfortable with that word because I'm his partner, of course I'm going to do this.

But everything changes, like intimacy.

We were still very close and intimate, but that was a big deal for him because we'd always had a lovely sex life.

We still had our lovely little rituals in the morning — even at [the hospital], I'd get him the coffee, I'd get him the papers, he could do the sudoku. He would do the "diabolical" sudoku without even using a pencil.

And while he was in the worst possible place, he was still trying to look after me too.

When he vomited at home, he'd never let me clean it up. I would be dry-reaching because that's the one bodily fluid I can't handle.

Friends who would come and see him told me afterwards, that he would whisper, "take care of her."

Their last trip to Wye River, on Victoria's Great Ocean Road, in November 2024. (Supplied: Hilda Quiroga)

Together at the pointy end

Steve mentioned voluntary assisted dying to his specialist about four months after being diagnosed.

It's a very legal process and then a pharmacist comes to your house with the medication.

That box of medication was here in the apartment for months.

Steve was then moved into palliative care and two weeks later during a terrible night, he said to me, "I think we're at the pointy end."

The next morning when the doctors were doing their rounds, he looked at me, I looked at him and he said to the doctor, "I've decided I want to use voluntary assisted dying today."

Right at the end it was just me, Steve's nephew, his partner and the VAD nurse.

He took his medication, swallowed it all in one go, and then had a bit of Coke because it's so vile.

Within about 20 minutes, he started to fall into unconsciousness.

I didn't cry. I just held Steve in my arms and just whispered in his ears as he passed away, because I thought he doesn't need to hear me sobbing, not now.

All I wanted him to hear was my voice saying, "It's all right, love. It's time. You're tired. It's time to rest."

He took his last breath. I listened to his heart. I loved falling asleep on his chest to hear that beautiful steady beat and it was gone.

Then I lost it.

Hilda Quiroga says Steve Mayer was a completely selfless, glorious and funny human. (Supplied: Hilda Quiroga)

18 months without Steve

I'm 18 months down the track and I still cry every day. I shed tears all over Melbourne.

[But] there's comfort in knowing he decided when he had had enough. Our apartment is just full of him. He's everywhere.

I've still got like his death T-shirt and I sleep with it every night and I haven't washed it. It's probably very unhygienic. My friend also nicked the pillow he died on and I sleep with that too.

We would hold hands when we fell asleep every night. He would tell me that he loved me every night and not just, "Love you, babe." He would turn around, face me and look me intently in the eyes and tell me how much he loved me.

Even though I've lost him and he's gone, I still feel obviously blessed and fortunate that I had that big love.

I think we all want that love and I'm a better person for meeting him. So, where there's grief, there's love.

title: Infantino denies 'defamatory' affair claims made in British newspaper
text:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who has endured a week of scathing criticism revolving around the now shelved private investment plan for the World Cup, has been accused by a British newspaper of paying off an alleged lover while at UEFA.

According to The Daily Telegraph, the Italian-Swiss lawyer, who served as secretary general of European football's governing body from 2009 to 2016, also previously used his influence to secure a promotion for the same UEFA employee with whom he was in an intimate relationship.

Infantino has categorically denied the allegations, according to the article which was published late on Friday.

When contacted by AFP on Saturday, a FIFA spokesperson had not responded.

According to The Telegraph, which did not cite its sources, this employee received a "a six-figure sum" upon her departure – at an unspecified time – in addition to the payment of tuition fees for a business school amounting to around 45,000 British pounds ($85,900).

Gianni Infantino (right) in 2007 when he was UEFA's deputy general secretary. (Getty Images: Etsuo Hara)

When contacted by AFP, UEFA acknowledged that "a departure payment was made to the individual in question" at that time, "coupled with the payment of fees for an MBA course at a local business school".

However, it insisted "the payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time", before adding that "such regulations have been tightened since 2016".

Quoted by The Telegraph, a FIFA spokesperson stated that Infantino, who has been married since 2001, "strongly denies these allegations", which were "categorically untrue".

"Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," FIFA added.

"No employee at UEFA and FIFA has ever raised a complaint regarding Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."

Infantino, who is standing for re-election next March, has been embroiled in a crisis since the announcement late last month of his controversial — and ultimately abandoned — plan to open up the World Cup to private investors.

He faces opposition in particular from UEFA, which on Thursday stood by its threat to boycott the World Cups, deeming the mere withdrawal of the controversial plan to be insufficient.

Infantino maintains substantial support

Following a crisis meeting in Morocco on Wednesday, FIFA apologised to its 211 member associations for mistakes in the handling of the proposal and said its leadership had reaffirmed its full support for Infantino.

The fallout has cast a shadow over Infantino's bid for a fourth term at the FIFA Congress in Morocco next year. No clear candidate to challenge him has yet emerged.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino (left) has faced criticism from President of the Football Association of Norway Lise Klaveness (right). (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

UEFA has said it no longer has confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation President Lise Klaveness called for him to resign on Friday, saying he no longer had the institutional trust required to govern FIFA.

But Infantino continues to enjoy substantial support among FIFA's 211 members. The Confederation of African Football (CAF) unanimously backed his leadership on Thursday, while South America's CONMEBOL rejected any attempt to oust him that did not involve a vote of all FIFA members.

Mexico's football federation (FMF) also backed Infantino, despite its regional confederation CONCACAF having called for a "comprehensive reckoning" with his presidency.

"The FMF will neither recognise nor approve any process convened outside of that institutional framework," the Mexican federation said.

AFP/Reuters

title: Workers down tools for second time at BHP's Port Hedland operations
text:
Workers at Australia's most lucrative port operations will walk off the job for a second day, amid an escalating industrial dispute.

The partial strike action at the port yesterday descended into a full stoppage after workers were allegedly threatened with no pay by mining giant BHP.

"BHP must understand that the Combined Ports Unions will not be deterred by threats or intimidation," AWU state secretary Craig Beveridge said.

BHP's Port Hedland operations. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

BHP rejected the claim, arguing the 47 work activities the AWU advised were subject to the ban on loading left employees with no work to do.

"Workplace laws are clear that we are not required to pay for the portion of an employee's work that is subject to an industrial ban," BHP said in a statement on Saturday.

Bargaining for a separate agreement, BHP high voltage workers responsible for Newman's electricity supply, about 450 kilometres inland from Port Hedland, are downing tools in a 12 hour work stoppage.

Ship loading continued

BHP said ships continued to be loaded during yesterday's stoppage.

"Vessels are being loaded, with scheduled departures subject to usual port planning and tides," a statement read.

Multiple bulk carriers could be seen departing BHP berths.

Ships being loaded with iron ore at Port Hedland on Saturday despite industrial action. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Speaking on Saturday morning, AMWU WA secretary Steve McCartney said he expected more than a hundred workers would take part in today's industrial action.

The Town of Port Hedland said it had no part to play, but acknowledged the action could cause unease.

"This is a matter between BHP, its workforce and their representatives, and the Town has no role in enterprise bargaining negotiations," chief executive Dale Stewart said.

"We recognise that many residents, businesses and community organisations have strong connections to the resources sector, and any significant industrial dispute can create uncertainty across the community."

Dale Stewart is the CEO of the Town of Port Hedland. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

No end in sight

Negotiations between the unions began last October, with the 11 bargaining meetings held so far failing to end in an agreement.

In July, unionised workers participated in an eight-hour strike which the ABC understands did not cause major disruptions for BHP.

Unionised workers participated in an eight-hour strike in Port Hedland in July. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

Unions have not ruled out further strikes, despite both the Combined Ports Unions and BHP alluding to positive progress in a bargaining meeting with the Fair Work Commission earlier this week.

BHP has committed to tabling an updated proposal at the next bargaining meeting with the Fair Work Commission on August 18.

title: Greens draw betting perk line ahead of gambling showdown
text:
The Greens have drawn a firm line on betting perks, clarifying they will not vote for the government's gambling legislation as it currently stands ahead of a political showdown when parliament returns this week.

The draft legislation is friendless in its current form, with the Coalition, Greens and crossbenchers all calling for sweeping amendments to ensure children and vulnerable Australians are protected from gambling harm.

Inducements became a stronger point of contention after a two-day Senate inquiry revealed allegations gambling company employees had provided VIP punters with perks including illegal drugs and escorts to encourage further gambling.

Betting giants denied the claims but the explosive testimony intensified calls for tougher reforms and bans on such practices, even drawing support from several Labor backbenchers.

Labor MPs call for tougher gambling reforms The Albanese government faces internal pressure to strengthen its gambling reforms, with more MPs calling for sweeping amendments.

Greens communication spokesperson Sarah Hanson-Young said promotions in which punters get their money back if their horse comes second rather than winning, "absolutely" need to go.

"Give me a freaking break," she told ABC's Insiders this morning.

"I think they use every trick in the book to promote and it's a real predatory nature, whether it's special deals, whether it's extra credits, whether it's favours to events.

"Inducements need to be off the table."

The position is in line with the late Peta Murphy's landmark parliamentary report on gambling reform, tabled in June 2023.

The report called for the abolition of inducements, defining it as "advertising and direct messaging [including] offers such as deposit matches, multi-bets, bonus bets, rewards programs and early cash-outs".

Senator Hanson-Young accused the government of "playing games", urging it to stand up for vulnerable Australians or risk the Greens' support.

"I'm not prepared to vote for what's on the table at the moment," she said.

Jenny McAllister says the government is open to "sensible amendments". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister defended the government's reforms, arguing "we're trying to get a good balance".

She said Labor had got it "broadly right" but was "open to sensible amendments" as negotiations with the Coalition and crossbench continue.

Communications Minister Anika Wells has previously stated the government was waiting to see formal amendments from the Coalition and Greens before locking in debate around the legislation.

'Partial bans do not work'

Labor's plan to combat harms from gambling, which costs Australians $32 billion in losses each year, includes a partial advertisement ban.

It would restrict gambling ads on TV to three per hour between 6am and 8:30pm, on radio during school pick-up and drop-off, as well as ban logos on sports players' jerseys or in stadiums.

Gambling company offered addict drugs Luke Bateman says gambling company employees unofficially offered him illicit drugs.

The partial ad ban, going against Murphy's recommendation of a phased, total ban, has drawn widespread criticism.

"It's really clear, partial bans do not work," Senator Hanson-Young said.

"In the absence of not tackling online advertising where it's the most insidious … this whole thing is set up to fail. We need proper bans on online advertising."

The Coalition has also spoken of tougher ad restrictions, with Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson stating the opposition would not support Labor's bill without changes but has not disclosed its demands.

title: Australian Beacroft smashes U20 world record to continue golden form
text:
Australia's Isaac Beacroft has maintained his stunning golden streak with a record-breaking victory in the 5km race walk at the world athletics under-20 championships in the US.

Beacroft's sizzling win in Eugene, Oregon, follows his Commonwealth Games gold medal just over a week ago in the 10km race walk in Glasgow.

Victory in Oregon means he now has the prestigious world U20 championships and Commonwealth Games gold-medal double.

​Beacroft also broke the world record in Oregon at the famous Hayward Field, his time of 18:40.37 smashing more than seven seconds off the previous mark.

"I'm over the moon, I couldn't be happier," the Australian said after his stunning victory on Saturday (local time).

"I knew coming in it was going to be so hard. It definitely was pretty hard, so I'm just so happy to get it done.

"It's a massive relief. I felt a fair bit of pressure going into this one, you are a Commonwealth champion, [people think] surely it's a walk in the park to do juniors.

"It's definitely not. I have raced each race to its merits, I don't know what is harder.

"I'm stoked to have won both, that's all I can say on that.''

Beacroft's world-record time meant he beat silver medallist Huajia Pu by more than three seconds, the Chinese athlete clocking 18:43.70.

Third place went to Italy's Nicolo' Vidal, more than 12 seconds behind in a time of 18:56.19.

Despite the impressive nature of his victory, Beacroft said it was difficult to come straight from Glasgow to Oregon.

"I had a day or two after my race to try and freshen up,'' he said.

"I didn't really freshen up there, I went out with the Commonwealth Games boys and girls.

"I didn't go too hard on the partying, but there was some definitely done, then it was pretty rough to travel here.

"There was a delay with the plane, but I think getting here and getting around the whole team has given me a real lift."

In another impressive result, the Australian team of Thewbelle Philp, Zara Hagan, Grace Crowe and Emilia Reed won their heat of the women's 4x100m sprint.

title: Planes in tarmac near miss at Sydney Airport
text:
The ABC understands a Jetstar plane has been involved in a near miss with a Qatar Airways plane on the tarmac at Sydney Airport this morning.

A Jetstar cabin crew worker was injured and assessed by paramedics. No passengers were injured.

The Jetstar A320 plane had to brake suddenly to avoid colliding with the Boeing 777 about 7am, with both planes stopping abruptly.

The Gold Coast-bound flight, JQ402, was taxiing to the runway when the incident occurred.

The ABC understands air traffic control was under operating restrictions from 6am to 8am this morning, reducing the number of planes flying in and out of the airport.

"Our aircraft was following instructions by Air Traffic Control when the pilots were forced to brake firmly after another aircraft came in close proximity," a Jetstar spokesperson said.

"We have commenced an investigation into the incident."

Airservices Australia said in a statement that Air Traffic Flow Management measures had been put in place following the incident, including departure spacing "to safely manage projected airborne and departure demands".

"We are working with airlines to reduce delays and the impact on passenger travel as much as possible," they said in a statement.

"Airservices is reviewing the incident and will assist with any safety investigation."

It comes after the air traffic safety body on Saturday said it was "working to address rostering issues" amid delays on the runway for multiple days in a row.

More than 150 flights were impacted as a result of roster constraints affecting the airport.

An investigation is also underway by the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) who said there was "damage to the connection between the 777 nose gear and aircraft tug".

"The ATSB will collect available data from both aircraft, and air traffic control," they said.

"Investigators will also interview the involved flight crew, tug operators and air traffic controllers, plus other witnesses and involved parties, and collect relevant recorded information including CCTV footage."

title: Portrait of domestic life wins $40,000 photography prize
text:
Paul Knight, an artist from Ettalong Beach in New South Wales, has won the National Photography Prize from the Murray Art Museum Albury (MAMA).

It is Australia's longest-running acquisitive photographic award and offers the $40,000 Audray Banfield Award.





The Chamber Music series documents the life Paul Knight shares with his partner, Peter. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Allison Jess) Knight's winning series of work, titled Chamber Music, documents the domestic life he shares with his partner, Peter, and the way relationships are shaped every day.

Knight was one of the 12 finalists for the prize, alongside Alana Hunt, Alex Walker, Amalia Lindo, Arlo Mountford, David Stephenson, JD Reforma, Lisa Stonham, Marian Tubbs, Morgan Hogg, Nathanael Edwards, and Sarah Rhodes.

Works of the finalists can now be seen in the 2026 National Photography Prize exhibition.

The announcement was made at Saturday's opening of the event, where Morgan Hogg was also awarded the $5,000 Emerging Artist Award for their work Silver Tongues, exploring the mythology and storytelling of the Pacific.

Morgan Hogg won the $5,000 John and Margaret Baker Fellowship. (Supplied: MAMA Albury )

Through a traditional Cook Island dance, Hogg explores the role of the Momokē, the water people of the underworld, who lure the souls of those who are almost ready to move onto the next life.

More than 330 artists entered this year's competition, with a curatorial committee comprising MAMA CEO Blair French, 2024 National Photography Prize recipient Ellen Dahl, and MAMA First Nations Curator Alinta Maguire selecting the 12 finalists.

Part of Alana Hunt's work included 64 polaroids. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Allison Jess)

National Gallery of Victoria senior curator of photography Natasha Bullock selected the winner of the National Photography Prize and the Emerging Artist Award.

“The work really captures the freedom with which artists are working today," Ms Bullock said. "Photography can be intimate, it can be highly conceptual or technically experimental and it can embrace all of the above. What’s exciting is the way these finalists are bringing all of these possibilities together, and finding new ways to make us look and see."

The Hear No, See No, Speak No series by Nathanael Edwards. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Allison Jess)

Mr French said this year's finalists were from Far North Queensland, Tasmania, regional NSW, Sydney and Melbourne and had varied levels of experience, from early career to "40-plus years" in the industry.

"The work is diverse and covers many themes and concepts, including family history, intimate stories, memories, environment, cultural identity, and connections to place," said Mr French.

Mr French says MAMA has a reputation for having a significant photography collection. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Allison Jess)

Mr French said the biennial competition is unique, as it looks at a collection of the artist's work, created in the past two years, rather than just one piece.

"You have a range of works by an artist that give you pause to consider and that's pretty rare in art prizes," he said.

The powerhouse behind the prize

The National Photography Prize was first held by MAMA, then known as the Albury Regional Art Gallery, in 1983.

The idea came from the inaugural director of the gallery, the late Audray Banfield.

A 2004 portrait of the late Audray Banfield, who was a well-known advocate for photography. (Supplied: Jules Boag and Rita Lazauskas, MAMA Collection)

Over the years, Ms Banfield helped to build the museum's growing collection of contemporary photography, which today includes more than 600 works, including important pieces by Tracey Moffatt, Max Dupain, Richard Woldendorp and Phillip Quirk.

Mr French said Ms Banfield's name has officially been attached to the $40,000 award this year.

"The gallery was founded and opened in 1981, and that's when Audray decided to make photography a focus of the gallery, with an aim to build on a collection of national significance," he said.

"When Audray passed away in 2024, we found it was appropriate to honour her within the museum and within the photography community."

The $40,000 is funded by the MAMA Art Foundation, which is an entity separate to the museum and focused on fundraising and advocating for the museum and its collection.

The Albury Regional Art Gallery was officially renamed the Murray Art Museum Albury after renovations in 2015. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Allison Jess)

This year the award for the National Photography Prize was increased from $30,000 to $40,000.

"When we sat down with the foundation and talked about naming the main award after Audray, we also asked them to think about lifting the prize amount," Mr French said.

"It has sat at $30,000 for a while and the way the world is, to put a little bit more money into artists pockets is an important part of what we are trying to do."

The National Photography Prize exhibition is at MAMA until November 22.

title: Canberra apprenticeships hit a brick wall in the middle of construction boom
text:
Canberra is in the middle of a construction boom but if you're looking for a qualified bricklayer, there might be a bit of a wait.

Currently there are only seven apprentice bricklayers training in the ACT, according to Housing Industry Association executive director for the ACT and Southern NSW, Geordan Murray.

"That's alarming, and well below the level required," Mr Murray said.

While commercial developments and large infrastructure projects like light rail are keeping Canberra's construction industry strong as a whole, there's been a downturn in the building of houses.

Mr Murray said that at the same time, there had also been a dramatic drop in trade apprenticeships.

"There's been an increase of 10 per cent in the construction workforce but over that time there's been a drop in apprentices by 20 per cent," Mr Murray said.

Shortage leaves questions about trade's future

Daniel Swan says most bricklayers on site with him are now over 40. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

Swan Bricklaying founder Daniel Swan started laying bricks at 15, learning the trade from his father.

Twenty-five years on, the third-generation bricklayer said finding young people willing and able to stick with the job had never been harder.

"It's definitely hard to get hold of people," Mr Swan said.

"Had a few young ones come through — they sort of struggle just handling the pressure of bricklaying, I guess.

"It is a very manual trade, so they do struggle just coming out and doing it."

He said most bricklayers on site with him were over 40.

"I've got Jacob, he's 21, but there's a big gap between [Jacob, at] 21, and the next guy," Mr Swan said.

"I don't know what it's going to be like in 10 years' time."

'It's hard work, but it's really rewarding'

Third-year bricklaying apprentice Jacob Bill says the work is incredibly rewarding despite being hard on his body. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

For third-year bricklaying apprentice Jacob Bill, starting out in the industry "was a hard gig" but sticking it out was worth it.

"I was a little skinny boy, and it was hard to really get pushing wheelbarrows — but I kind of just stuck through it," Mr Bill said.

"It's tough on your body, it's hard work, but it's good — it's really rewarding.

" Seeing all the houses go up, seeing all the new suburbs going up you can see your work, and it just feels great. "

But the path to qualifying hasn't been straightforward for Mr Bill, having moved through three different crews during his apprenticeship.

He said time spent labouring instead of laying bricks did not give him the skills he was hoping to learn.

"As a second year, when you're labouring and you're not on the trowel, you don't develop that skill," Mr Bill said.

"It's really hard when you're a third year and you can't lay bricks properly — you need that skill straight away."

A shortage of skills, not labour

Bricklaying trainer Lynne Sheffield says she has been trying to help address the shortage of apprentices for 20 years. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Bricklayer Lynne Sheffield, founder of trade school Quality Training in Construction, said the shortage was not so much about the number of available labourers as it was the number trained in specific trade skills.

"We have a lot of labour, but not skilled labour. And that's what we really need, the skilled labour," Ms Sheffield said.

She has spent 30 years in the construction industry, and said she had seen this coming for some time.

"The last 20 years we've been going to the governments and everywhere saying that there's a massive shortage. That's why I went into education," Ms Sheffield said.

"Now what's happened; it's gotten a lot worse."

Despite being a qualified trade, there is currently no requirement to be licensed to work as a bricklayer in the ACT.

Canberra bricklayers are not required to have qualifications to work in the ACT. (ABC News: Jacqueline Lynch)

"We're not licensed at all. We don't even have to have our qualifications," Ms Sheffield said.

" When you look around the job sites, there's a lot of bad work — and they don't know what they're doing. They're not trained properly. "

Ms Sheffield said the current model — which sees apprentices split between limited classroom time and full days on site — was not giving them the grounding they needed before they were exposed to the pressures of a building site.

"I believe that they should bring them into the [trade] schools first and get them trained up," she said.

"Then they have resilience and they have skills, so when they get put out into the industry with the bosses, they're useful."

More tradies needed to meet housing target

Geordan Murray of the Housing Industry Association says a slow residential construction sector is part of what is driving the drop in apprentice numbers. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Mr Murray of the Housing Industry Association said one of the problems with the apprenticeship model was the high attrition.

"We see a lot more apprentices commencing than we do completing," he said.

" We really need to have opportunities for workers or young people … to get exposure to construction early on, so they're coming into the industry with their eyes open. "

Mr Murray said the drop in apprenticeships was driven by several factors, including a slow residential building sector.

"The residential building industry typically trains a larger share of apprentices in construction trades, and at the moment we've had a downturn of residential building," he said.

Geordan Murray says bricklaying has been hit hardest by the apprentice shortage, but all trades have seen a downturn in numbers. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

Mr Murray said businesses were reluctant to commit to a four-year apprenticeship without confidence there would be enough work in the pipeline to sustain it.

"What we need to see is ongoing employment opportunities for apprentices throughout the business cycle," he said.

"During an upswing in building activity, we'll see really strong demand from employers looking for apprentices.

"But during a cyclical downturn, like we're seeing now in residential building, we'll see more apprentices looking for work than there are opportunities."

Mr Murray said delivering the ACT government's 30,000-home commitment by 2030 would require more people entering the trades and more employers willing to train them, alongside a rethink of how apprenticeships are structured and supported.

"We have a real problem with an ageing workforce of bricklayers, and we simply aren't attracting enough new younger workers into the workforce to replace those who are reaching retirement age," Mr Murray said.

title: 'Always by my side': Argentina mourns death of Jorge Messi
text:
Jorge Messi, the father of soccer star Lionel Messi, has died at a hospital in the central Argentina city of Rosario. He was 68.

The Rosario-based Club Atlético Newell's Old Boys announced his death in a social media post on Saturday that said he had undergone treatment in recent months for an unspecified illness.

The post described him as "the pillar and the person who, with vision, rigour and affection, supported the career of the best player of all time, alongside his wife, Celia Cuccittini".

Lionel Messi embraces his father Jorge Messi after the World Cup final in Qatar in 2022. (Getty Images: Robert Michael)

In a statement, the South American Football Confederation (CONMEBOL) also offered its condolences "with respect and affection for Lionel".

Lionel Messi led Argentina to a runner-up finish in this year's World Cup. In the team's first match, against Algeria, he was visibly emotional after scoring the first of his three goals. He said later that he wept for "a reason unrelated to sports".

"I went through some difficult, complicated days," he said.

"I am grateful to the delegation, to all my teammates, because they were always by my side wishing me strength so that I would be OK."

Media reports at the time outraged the Messi family, which days later released a statement confirming that "Jorge is experiencing a health issue", without specifying the nature of his condition.

"A person's health and the peace of mind of their loved ones should not be the subject of speculation or irresponsible media interest," according to the statement, which also expressed "discomfort at the lack of sensitivity, respect and scruples with which some people have treated a strictly private and family matter".

A minute of silence is held in memory of Jorge Messi, Leo Messi's father, during the FVG Cup match between Udinese Calcio and Nottingham Forest in Italy. The FVG Cup is a three team tournament that also includes Barcelona. (Getty Images: Mattia Radoni/NurPhoto)

Jorge Messi was a chemical technician and worked as a steelworker. He played soccer as a midfielder and reached the youth ranks of Newell's Old Boys but had to abandon the sport to complete his mandatory military service in Argentina.

He played a fundamental role in his third son's career, serving as his agent and managing his business affairs.

He was the one who travelled with a young Messi to Barcelona in the early 2000s for the trial that would open the doors to La Masia, the club's youth academy.

Lionel Messi made his professional debut in 2005 and went on to win eight Ballon d'Or awards. He led Argentina to the 2022 World Cup title.

Lionel Messi (back) poses with his family, including dad Jorge (centre) in 2003. (Getty Images: Marcelo Boeri/El Grafico)

"My dad was always by my side," Lionel Messi said in a 2007 interview with Radio del Plata.

"Sometimes I would lock myself in my room to cry when we arrived in Barcelona, or my dad would do the same without me seeing him, or thinking I didn't see him. We pretended we were both OK, but we weren't.

"My dad even asked me what I wanted to do when we were feeling down, if I wanted to stay or go back, and I wanted to stay, and he stayed with me."

His father negotiated the contracts with Barça and later his transfers to Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami, while also managing the use of his famous son's image rights and his numerous investments in real estate, hotels and restaurants.

In 2013, father and son were accused by a Spanish prosecutor of trying to conceal earnings from the player's image rights. Jorge Messi paid more than 5 million euros ($8.1 million) on August 14 to cover alleged back taxes and interest.

In Rosario, a sign at the VIP Rosario restaurant, one of the Messi family's gastronomic ventures, indicated that it was closed for the day.

The president of Argentina's soccer federation, Claudio Tapia, on Saturday issued a lengthy statement in which he recognised Jorge Messi "for having raised a person of values: humble, respectful, and deeply committed to others".

The organisation ordered a moment of silence to be observed at all matches across all categories of Argentine soccer and mandated that players, referees and coaching staff wear black armbands.

title: Historic farm's sale to carbon credit company raises community ire
text:
The sale of a historic Victorian high country cattle station to a carbon fund manager has raised concerns among residents and a federal MP about the property's future.

Cobungra Station, which has been farming cattle for more than 170 years near Omeo, has been sold to specialist carbon fund and asset manager Silva Capital.

Silva Capital creates and manages Australian Carbon Credit Units projects as part of the federal government's Carbon Credit Scheme.

Credits are generated through land reforestation and other agricultural projects that support the transition to net zero.

Carbon farming projects have become common in Australia, as companies look for quality carbon capture projects. (ABC News: Melanie Arnost, file photo)

The fund has confirmed plans to transform the station, running a carbon project alongside cattle farming.

"It's been done in several locations across Victoria and throughout Australia," Silva Capital co-managing director Raphael Wood said.

"What we've aimed to prove here is that food and fibre and carbon sequestration biodiversity can go hand in hand and create a more sustainable agricultural system," he said.

The transformation will see more native vegetation planted on the farm.

Raphael Wood says the fund will work with the local community to ensure all concerns around the Cobungra sale are addressed. (Supplied: Stephen Blake)

"We work with local experts, local community, the people who've worked that station before, to learn from them how to maximise the productivity and bring in new science and new techniques, for open woodland integrated with pasture to improve hopefully the productivity on site," Mr Wood said.

What's lost?

The deal has been approved by the Foreign Investment Review Board, and the sale of the farm is imminent.

However, some community members fear the project will result in a shift in Cobungra's identity.

Dianne Carroll is a local historian from nearby Omeo.

She said Cobungra had special significance for the local area.

"Slowly we are seeing the demise of many farms and that history is an important part of our culture, and it should be retained," Ms Carroll said.

"I'm not arguing against the conservation or protection of our environment, but I'm questioning whether productive, historical, significant country is the appropriate place to permanently convert land for the generation of carbon credits," she said.

The Coalition has called on the government to reject the proposal.

Cobungra lies in the electorate of the federal opposition agriculture spokesperson Darren Chester.

He said the decision to allow the proposal distorted the market for anyone who wished to buy land for traditional agricultural purposes.

"The individual or the farming organisation who might want to come along and continue to use the property for just mainstream agricultural production will be outbid by an organisation relying on government subsidies and schemes to fund their purchases," Mr Chester said.

Darren Chester says selling farms for carbon projects sets a worrying precedent. (Supplied: Darren Chester)

Mr Chester drew on the recent example of the sale of Tasmania's biggest farm, Rushy Lagoon, to a British investor, which was partially funded through the federal government's Clean Energy Finance Corporation.

He said the cumulative impact of large farms being acquired under the government's model deserved closer consideration.

"What is the long-term ambition for these carbon credit type sales? How many millions of hectares of productive agricultural land will we lose before it's in the national interest?" he said.

Mr Wood said the fund was looking forward to engaging with the local community about any concerns they had over the process.

"We intend to reach out to the community and start engaging and learning from the community about how we can maintain the agricultural productivity of Cobungra, and introduce them to what we are trying to achieve with Silva and Cobungra," he said.

A chance to diversify

Not all agree that carbon farming and traditional agriculture are at odds.

Farmers for Climate Action chief executive Verity Morgan-Schmidt said carbon farming could coexist with traditional farming, and helped diversify farmers' income.

Verity Morgan-Schmidt says carbon farming and more traditional farming can co-exist. (Supplied: Farmers for Climate Action)

"To me, that represents the opportunity that is actually increasingly coming down the pipeline for Australian producers to be able to diversify their income streams and actually, over the longer term, look to strengthen the resilience of their properties and regions as well," she said.

"It's really about a revenue diversification opportunity for farmers, provided we get their methodologies right and make sure that farmers are able to manage the access into that market as well."

The Clean Energy Finance Corporation has confirmed it is not involved in the purchase of Cobungra.

The Federal Government has been contacted for comment.

title: Trams are running but the Gold Coast's light rail fight is not over
text:
After $1.55 billion and four years of disruptive construction, the Gold Coast's latest mass transit system has finally begun taking passengers.

Light rail stage 3 has connected the bustling shopping precinct of Broadbeach to the stunning beaches of Burleigh Heads.

The state government estimates two million passengers will use the network every month but the light rail has become a symbol of the city's struggle to manage population growth.

Locals know the trams carry big change.

Decades in the making

Urban planning consultant Ned Wales worked at Gold Coast City Council in the mid-2000s, as detailed planning for light rail began.

"Light rail has a dedicated right of way; you get the reliability in terms of timing and scheduling," he said.

"[It's] not cheap but it's certainly been well worth it."

Associate Professor Ned Wales from Bond University. (ABC: Glenn Mullane)

The first stage — a 13-kilometre line from Gold Coast University Hospital to Broadbeach — took three years to build and cost $1.61 billion in today's dollars.

The former Labor state government initially estimated the 6.7km stage 3 would cost $709 million.

That has since blown-out to $1.55 billion.

Mr Wales, now an Assistant Professor of Sustainable Development at Bond University, said light rail required costly upgrades to underground sewer and water infrastructure — with "many, many moving parts" involved.

An aerial shot of the Stage 3 light rail construction, looking north from Miami to Mermaid Beach. (Supplied: GoldLinQ)

In September 2025, light rail operator GoldLinQ said 48km of utilities had been relocated or upgraded and 137 power poles installed to build 60 per cent of stage 3.

GoldLinQ chair John Witheriff said crews were uncovering decades-old infrastructure, including broken asbestos-cement water pipes, adding unexpected delays.

"We've got no idea what's underground in our city and we've got no idea how long the stuff's been in there and when it's all going to break up," he said at the time.

Disruption and reflection

Those disruptions came at a cost for many businesses along the route.

Jess Firkin relocated his vintage clothing shop from the light rail route in Mermaid Beach south to Miami last year.

"When something happens to you, you're very quick to make judgement and point figures," he said.

"But that doesn't get the bills paid."

Jess Firkin at his old shopfront at Mermaid Beach last year, prior to moving. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Now about 100 metres off the new light rail route, Mr Firkin said his trade had increased by 70 per cent.

"As much as it does suck for things to happen outside of your control, there are always actions you can take to help rectify those situations," he said.

"I would really like it to end on a positive note and really emphasise that business owners need to take accountability and that's my biggest lesson."

Construction of light rail at Mermaid Beach, in April 2025. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Locals Raeleigh and Russell Olive said the construction process has been "a real mess".

"The restrictions on getting in and out of Burleigh [are] … gone and it looks good again," Ms Olive said.

"It's one of our favourite places to come, so it's nice to know that other people will be enjoying it as well."

But Mr Olive said "it would have been a great idea" to extend the line further south to the airport.

Opposition builds, plans get scrapped

Light rail was not meant to end with stage 3.

Stage 4 would have connected Burleigh Heads to the airport, described as a critical part of the entire network by urban planners.

But the cancellation of stage 4 came about after once-sleepy coastal villages along the proposed route became the focus of intense high-rise development.

The light rail ends at Burleigh Heads, instead of extending further south to the airport, as planned. (Graphic: ABC News)

Opposition grew in suburbs such as Palm Beach, where "Trams Outta Palmy" signs appeared outside homes and shops.

Even surfing great Mick Fanning voiced his disapproval online.

While he supported stage 4, Mr Wales said "the downside is gentrification".

"Real estate values increase particularly around tram stations," he said. "That may lead to some displacement of those on lower socio-economic incomes."

Opposition to light rail on the southern Gold Coast has been vocal, with protests seen here in 2021. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

The LNP government cancelled stage 4 last year, citing local opposition and an estimated cost of $5.7 billion to $9.8 billion.

But on Friday, Queensland Labor senator Murray Watt said the state had not given the Commonwealth a firm stage 4 business case, making it "impossible to say exactly what that cost would be".

The state has preserved the light rail corridor along the southern Gold Coast, leaving the door open for a future government to revive the project.

What's next?

A network of larger buses dubbed the "GC Surfer" will carry passengers south of Burleigh Heads, but without the dedicated lanes to bypass traffic.

The GC Surfer will also link the Gold Coast's inland suburbs, including Nerang and Robina, which would not have been feasible with light rail.

"Those communities sandwiched between light rail and heavy [rail] will now have the opportunity to enjoy both," Burleigh MP Hermann Vorster said.

An artist's impression has been released, but costs for the "GC Surfer" bus are yet to be finalised. (Supplied: Queensland Government)

Labor's only Gold Coast MP, Meaghan Scanlon, called the stage 3 launch without an airport extension "bittersweet" but stopped short of committing to stage 4.

With the city's population expected to reach one million in the next two decades, Mr Wales said the Gold Coast's "hesitation" towards public transport must change.

"If you look at any major city around the world, their mass transit is crucially important in terms of efficiency and economic development," he said.

"For us to be more prosperous, light rail is part of the solution."

title: NFL star uses Hall of Fame speech to announce he has dementia
text:
Former star NFL running back Roger Craig has revealed during his induction speech into the Pro Football Hall of Fame that he has vascular dementia.

The former San Francisco 49ers player spoke in a pre-recorded video message while he sat on stage wearing his gold jacket at Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium in Canton, Ohio.

Presented by former teammate Jamie Williams, he received a standing ovation from the crowd and hugs from the many Hall of Famers on stage.

Nearly eight minutes into a nine-minute speech, Craig announced his diagnosis, saying his doctors believe "it may be related, at least in part, to the concussions" he experienced during his playing career.

"The changes were gradual," Craig said.

"At first, they were easy to dismiss as normal aging. Over time, my family noticed, too."

Symptoms of vascular dementia, according to the Mayo Clinic, include confusion; trouble finding the right words; difficulty paying attention; trouble organising thoughts or actions; difficulty planning and following through with plans; slowed thinking; uncertainty about what to do next; and memory issues.

Roger Craig was a trailblazer at the running back position for the San Francisco 49ers. (Getty Images: George Rose)

"Two things could be true," Craig said.

"Football gave me opportunities beyond anything I can imagine. It helped shape the man I became.

"At the same time, we know more today about brain health than when I played. I hope sharing my story encourages people to pay attention to their health and seek help when something doesn't feel right.

"I want people to know that this diagnosis doesn't define me. I am still Roger Craig. I am still a father, still a husband, a teammate, a friend and someone who loves this game and the people who brought it to my life.

Inside a brain with suspected CTE The effect of head knocks over Gordi Kirkbank-Ellis's decades-long sporting career isn't immediately obvious. That is, until you see what's happening to his brain.

"If sharing my story helps even one family or one former player, then it's worth it. Football gave me everything: opportunity, discipline, lifelong friends and the platform to grow as a man. This honour belongs to my parents who started it all."

Selected by the 49ers in the second round of the 1983 draft as a fullback out of Nebraska, Craig become one of the most versatile players in league history.

He excelled as a runner, receiver and blocker, helping the 49ers win three of their five Super Bowls.

In 1985, Craig became the first player in NFL history to have 1,000 yards rushing and 1,000 yards receiving in a season.

Craig was selected from the seniors category and entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame Class of 2026 with Drew Brees, Larry Fitzgerald, Luke Kuechly and Adam Vinatieri.

title: Exhausted Vollering reclaims yellow jersey with one stage remaining
text:
Demi Vollering launched a blistering attack to win the eighth stage of the Tour de France Femmes and take the yellow jersey heading into tonight's final stage.

The Dutchwoman upped the pace on the fourth and final small climb and title rival Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney cracked with about 6km to go, sitting back down in her saddle as 2023 Tour winner Vollering surged ahead.

As Vollering zoomed along the famed Promenade des Anglais by the seaside in Nice, Niewiadoma-Phinney and former Giro d'Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini could not close the gap.

Demi Vollering collapses to the ground in a ice vest after a gruelling stage. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

"It's funny but only this morning I saw myself taking the yellow jersey," Vollering said.

"I thought it might come true, that maybe that's the way things should be. During the day, I tried to remind myself I could do it."

So it proved.

Vollering raised her arms in triumph at the line, then collapsed to the ground and panted heavily as she tried to get her breath back.

"I was in so much pain, I can hardly describe it, but I made it happen," Vollering said.

"This goes to prove that if you really believe in something, if you dream big, it doesn't matter how much risk you take or how much pain you have to go through."

Longo Borghini was second and Niewiadoma-Phinney was third, both 17 seconds behind. The day belonged to Vollering, who won the Giro d'Italia this year to complete the hat-trick of Grands Tour wins.

She is eight seconds ahead of Niewiadoma-Phinney, the 2024 champion, in the overall standings. The Polish rider took the yellow jersey with a brilliant solo win up Mont Ventoux a day earlier, and rode a yellow bike to go with it on Stage 8.

The 172km route from Sisteron to Nice on the south-east coast was mostly flat for sprinters but featured four minor climbs which made it a little more tricky.

With the main title contenders initially saving energy for tonight's tough-looking decisive stage in the hills around Nice, the yellow jersey group let Frenchwoman Maeva Squiban and Dutchwoman Loes Adegeest form a long breakaway.

Squiban slid off her bike heading into a turn on a downhill section and landed heavily on her left side. She had cuts and grazes and screamed in agony as a medic on a motorbike tried bandaging her arm while she was riding.

She carried on riding despite the pain while, up ahead, Adegeest was caught inside the last 9km.

Defending champion withdraws

Pauline Ferrand-Prévôt pulled out of the race shortly before the stage after feeling unwell.

The French rider's Visma-Lease a Bike team said on X that the decision to pull her out of the race was made after consultation with the team's medical staff.

Why broadcasting row has Tour de France Femmes fans 'pissed off' In the Tour de France Femmes, less than 40 seconds separates the top three riders with only two stages to go. That's just one reason why supporters are questioning why they can't watch the entire race.

The 2024 Paris Olympic champion in mountain biking won the Tour de France Femmes on her debut last year. But she struggled this year and was in 14th place overall before withdrawing.

The final stage tonight features four sharp climbs of Col d'Èze, which is nestled in the hills overlooking the tiny Principality of Monaco.

Two years ago, Niewiadoma-Phinney beat Vollering on a final day mountain stage to win the race by just four seconds.

Vollering will have to ensure it is not a case of déjà vu.

"Tomorrow's course is going to be super hard," she said.

"We knew it from the beginning of the Tour."

title: Side dish vegetable takes the spotlight as vegetable of the year
text:
A vegetable that is more known as a side dish than the main character is back in the spotlight.

Surging searches for cabbage on Google and Pinterest have driven media outlets Vogue and The New York Times to name cabbage the vegetable of the year.

Cabbage, a member of the brassica family like broccoli and kale, has long been celebrated for its variety of uses from coleslaw to cabbage rolls.

Duncan Welgemoed was first introduced to sugarloaf cabbage while working in the UK. (Supplied: Duncan Welgemoed)

But top chefs such as Duncan Welgemoed from Africola in Adelaide are part of a growing fanbase for sugarloaf cabbage, a conical-shaped variety that is getting a cult-like status.

"It's one of our most popular vegetables for sure," he said.

"I think some people haven't had sugarloaf cabbage before, but it is incredibly moreish.

" We go through hundreds a week. "

So what does it taste like? It has less sulphur and more sweetness than your traditional cabbage.

At his restaurant, Mr Welgemoed serves sugarloaf cabbage roasted in butter and thyme, seasoned with salt and pepper, and finished with a Caesar dressing.

Loading...

The vegetable is a versatile addition to any home chef's repertoire, according to Mr Welgemoed.

"They're delicate enough to eat raw and they're hardy enough to really roast," he said.

"When you buy it, it's enough for two people as opposed to when you buy a savoy cabbage or a white cabbage, you've got to find multiple uses for it within your cooking week because they're so large.

"With the sugarloaf cabbage, that's a one-and-done."

Sweet, nutritious, cheap

As a long-time fan of sugarloaf cabbage, Mr Welgemoed said it had become easier to source in recent years.

"They used to be super hyper-seasonal; you could only get them in Australia for like once a year in very short bursts," he said.

"But then, due to demand and popularity, particularly from the commercial side, we started to see more and more through the market."

Penny Reidy says sugarloaf cabbage is a relatively cheap and versatile option. (Supplied: Penny Reidy)

SA Produce Markets marketing manager Penny Reidy said it was good to see a "forgotten" vegetable like cabbage rise in popularity.

She said sugarloaf cabbage could be used in many ways and nutritionally, it was a great source of vitamin C and fibre.

"People that are a little bit more adventurous and don't just want their normal greens on their salads or in their stir-fries can finely slice it instead of using lettuce," she said.

"You add it to your burgers, you wrap your sandwich [in it], stir-fry it, grill it or roast wedges with olive oil, but you can also add it to soups and casseroles or cold sauce."

Sugarloaf cabbage (not pictured) has less sulphur and more sweetness than traditional cabbage. (ABC News: Adel Fruean)

Beyond the nutritional benefits, Ms Reidy said sugarloaf cabbage was a relatively cheap option that had a long shelf life.

"If you buy it and think you're going to do something with but then you forget for a week, the good thing is that it's not going to go rotten overnight," she said.

" So there's definitely some demand there for it in the cost-of-living crisis that we're having and for people looking to stretch their budget. "

Sourcing sugarloaf

Despite a growing interest in sugarloaf cabbage among foodies, finding a farmer that grows them is tricky.

Paul Schreurs is the youngest son of three brothers in Peter Schreurs and Sons, who have grown cabbage their whole lives at a farm in Devon Meadows, just outside Melbourne.

Paul Schreurs at his farm in Devon Meadows, about 50km south-east of Melbourne. (Supplied: Schreurs & Sons)

He said the family had experimented with other cabbage varieties, including Chinese and mini cabbage, before specialising in sugarloaf.

The second-generation Victorian farmer described it as sweet and versatile.

"It's very palatable eating it raw and it cooks up very easily, so it's not like your old tough drumhead cabbage that needs a lot of cooking," Mr Schreurs said.

" I believe it's the best-tasting cabbage out of all of them. "

Mr Schreurs said while sugarloaf could be grown year-round, farmers could be reluctant to invest in supply if the demand was not strong enough to scale up production.

He added that sometimes, consumers who had only purchased sugarloaf because other types of cabbage were not available ended up being converted to sugarloaf.

"Our biggest success with sugarloaf cabbage getting more customers on board is when there's been a shortage of other cabbages," he said.

"They've then discovered, 'Oh, this is actually quite a good cabbage' and we've had a lot of repeat sales."

title: Melbourne Royal Show could cancel poultry exhibition amid bird flu fears
text:
Victoria's iconic agricultural show could be without bird exhibitions and poultry competitions as avian flu spreads across the state.

The Melbourne Royal Show is understood to be meeting on Monday to discuss the upcoming show and whether the exhibitions will be scrapped for the second time in three years.

The show, scheduled for September 24 to October 4, traditionally brings hundreds of birds together at the poultry pavilion for exhibitions and judging.

Hundreds of birds are brought to the Melbourne Royal Show each year for competitions and exhibitions. (Supplied: Melbourne Royal Show)

Victoria's chief veterinary officer introduced on Friday a temporary poultry housing requirement in high-risk areas, requiring poultry owners with 50 or more birds in metropolitan Melbourne, coastal areas, and some neighbouring areas to house birds to reduce contact with wild birds.

There are now 215 confirmed cases of H5N1 bird flu in wild birds across Australia, but no detections have been confirmed in poultry.

Breeders fear birds will be put at risk

The Victorian Poultry Fanciers Association (VPFA) said it expected the Melbourne Royal Show to cancel the bird exhibitions at Monday's meeting.

VPFA secretary Andrea Beaty said even with ramped-up biosecurity protocols across the south of the state, exhibitors did not want to risk their flocks.

"I've got years of breeding in my birds, and I'm not losing that," she said.

Ms Beaty said as a poultry breeder she had started to house her birds inside a shed as a preventative measure.

"I've been talking to VPFA members, and their feeling is to cancel further shows. The cases are increasing on a daily basis," she said.

"As for the Melbourne Royal [Show], I work there as an attendant. My advice is they're having a meeting on Monday; I suspect that show will be cancelled. We're six to seven weeks out, there are a lot of cases, and I don't think they'll get the patronage of the exhibitors."

Melbourne Royal Show is still taking entry applications for its poultry competition. (Supplied: Melbourne Royal Show)

It is not the first time a biosecurity threat has shut down exhibitions at the Melbourne Royal Show. In 2024, an outbreak of avian influenza shut down poultry exhibitions as organisers tried to curb the spread of the disease.

Melbourne Royal Show general manager Hannah von Bibra said the health and welfare of animals, exhibitors and visitors to the show was the number one priority, with the show committee working with Agriculture Victoria to assess the unfolding risk.

"As the situation is still currently evolving, Melbourne Royal will take all necessary measures to ensure the safety and wellbeing of all animals, exhibitors and visitors to the show, and will make any decisions regarding our competition based on the advice from our partners," she said.

It follows an announcement on Friday that the Royal Adelaide Show would be cancelling its bird competitions ahead of next month's events due to bird flu concerns.

Biosecurity the best defence: Victoria's chief vet

There are 47 positive cases of H5N1 flu in wild birds in Victoria, with new detections at Yambuk, Apollo Bay and Clyde, in addition to known areas around Portland and Nelson.

Free-range egg farmers who move their hens indoors to protect them from H5 bird flu can continue to label and sell their eggs as free range.

Victorian chief veterinary officer Graeme Cooke said reducing contact between poultry and wild birds was "one of the most effective ways to lower the risk of the disease entering a flock".

Dr Cooke said producers were urged to maintain stringent biosecurity practices.

"This housing requirement provides an additional layer of protection in areas of increased risk," he said.

Victorian poultry producers will be forced to house their birds as H5 bird flu cases continue to climb. (ABC News)

Southern NSW and Northeast Victorian Poultry auctioneer Braham Metry said the restrictions posed a problem for free-range producers with large flocks.

"If you've got large commercial flocks, they've got to have enough shedding," he said.

"You can't build a chook shed overnight. If you've got 25–30,000 free-range hens and if you don't have the facilities to have them shedded permanently, you have got a problem."

He said the industry was well prepared from the previous H7 outbreak but that producers would be forced to "go with the flow".

"Whatever will happen, will happen," Mr Metry said.

"Last time we had bird flu, they shut all the auctions, I worked months without an income. No compensation if they close it down, so you just have to go with the flow. It's not worth worrying about."

Egg producers are bracing for a potential bird-flu outbreak among their flock (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Victorian Farmers Federation president Ryan Milgate said bird flu was not a surprise to the industry.

"It's something they've been watching closely for the last couple of years to be honest, with it moving around the world," he said.

"They've had a lot of time, and they're putting a lot of effort into being prepared and doing everything they can to make sure they can protect their birds and their farms as best as possible."

The new housing requirement is a change for some producers, but Mr Milgate said it was "the best possible defence at the current time against the bird flu for these guys".

"They're willing to do whatever it takes to protect their birds and their businesses," he said.

title: 'Unusual' flu trend with SA cases to spike later than expected
text:
An "unusual" flu trend will likely see more people sneezing and reaching for their tissues after the peak winter season, South Australia's health experts say.

SA's Chief Public Health Officer Nicola Spurrier said the number of flu cases have only just started picking up in the last few weeks in the state.

"We've had an unusual year, because we've only just started to see the flu numbers tick up — and look at us, we're in August," Professor Spurrier said.

"The most likely reason for that is, last year was again an unusual year.

"We had the standard peak right in the middle of winter… and then we saw a kick up around about October, going into summer we had another wave."

Nicola Spurrier says SA likely has strong immunity to flu over winter due to a surge of cases in summer 2025. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Professor Spurrier said the subclade K strain from the northern hemisphere, otherwise known as the "Super K" strain, contributed to the second wave of summer cases in Australia.

"What I think that's done is give our community at a population level — some immunity to flu, but with infectious diseases over a period of time — population immunity wanes," Professor Spurrier said.

Adelaide general practitioner Daniel Byrne said this year's flu cases were about 10 times less compared to previous winters.

"The world's changing … international travel, the spread of viruses around the world — when it's winter in the northern hemisphere it's summer here, perhaps we're getting more flu in our summer which is a total change from 15-20 years ago," Dr Byrne said.

"We might be in for a late season, so the big advice is, it's still not too late to get your flu shot because the flu could still be coming later this year."

Flu cases in SA have been unusually low so far this year. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Dr Byrne said other respiratory illnesses were keeping doctors busy.

"We're getting a lot of rhinovirus, which is the common cold — that's probably number one, the second would be RSV [respiratory syncytial virus]," he said.

So far this year, South Australia has recorded 5,702 cases of RSV, an illness that is highly contagious and is a common cause of hospitalisation in young babies.

Protecting against RSV

Dr Byrne said he would like to see expanded eligibility for the free RSV vaccine.

Pregnant women have had free access to the RSV vaccine under the National Immunisation Program since February 2025.

Newborns who did not receive protection during their mothers' pregnancy were eligible for the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab through state and territory-funded programs.

In May this year, adults over 75 became eligible for the free vaccine, which can cost up to $350, the WA government has expanded eligibility to include those aged 65 and older living in residential aged care.

Daniel Byrne says eligibility for the free RSV vaccine should be expanded. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Dr Byrne said he would like to see the same in SA.

"Personally, as a doctor in South Australia I would love to be able to give those vulnerable people an RSV vaccine, and save the health system a huge amount of money as well," he said.

Professor Spurrier said health authorities would be watching RSV case numbers in the year to come.

"Let's see how we go with this year and review those results, we always make comparisons of course we do when we look at epidemiology between states," she said.

title: Fijian rugby pro, 26, dies of suspected heat stroke after training
text:
Fijian rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi has died of suspected heat stroke after a training session in Japan. He was 26.

His death was announced on Saturday by his team, Kyushu Electric Power Kyuden Voltex — known as Kyushu KV.

The Japanese second-division club said Vunilagi died on Friday after falling ill on Monday and being hospitalised.

"After team practice on Monday … Saimoni displayed symptoms consistent with severe heat stroke," the team said in a statement Saturday.

"He was transported to a medical facility for treatment, but despite the best efforts of the medical team, he sadly passed away."

Kyushu KV is based in Fukuoka, a city in southwestern Japan. Temperatures there reportedly reached around 35C on Monday.

"The players, staff, and all team associates are devastated by this sudden news," the team said.

Back rower Vunilagi joined Kyushu KV last month, having previously played in the Japanese top flight with Tokyo Sungoliath.

"Although Saimoni had only recently joined Kyushu KV, his generous spirit and powerful style of play had raised high hopes for his contributions in the upcoming season," Kyushu KV added.

"We humbly pray for the repose of his soul and extend our heartfelt condolences to his bereaved family."

The club supplied no other details surrounding the death.

Erone Fitzpatrick is a star – All-Australian, Carlton leader and selected in the Irish representative AFLW side – but there’s one thing about Australian rules football that leaves her baffled. Club loyalty – or rather, the lack of it. Hailing from County Laois in Ireland, Fitzpatrick helped lead them to their first Gaelic football title in over 20 years in 2022, before being poached by Carlton for the 2023 season. Carlton’s Erone Fitzpatrick will represent her homeland in the ALFW Aus vs Ireland clash. Joe Armao She played with the same teammates from age four to 23; switching clubs or counties is “unheard of at home”. “Talking to a lot of the Aussies here, they can’t get over how loyal you are to your club and your county throughout your whole career,” Fitzpatrick said. “I would play with the one club for my whole football career, and I would play with the one county for my whole football career, and they couldn’t get over that.

Advertisement

“That’s why we find it really strange, the whole trade period and people leaving clubs and going to different clubs and stuff like that.” Fitzpatrick hopes she can stick with her AFLW side in a similar way. “I would love that,” she said. “You never know what can happen in the future, but I think it would be very weird for me to go anywhere else. I think if you asked a lot of the Irish players, they would say the exact same thing.” Since the AFLW’s inaugural season in 2017, the presence of Gaelic football cross-coders has skyrocketed, with 44 active Irish players in the league and two inactive. Their effect has been profound. The Irish players play a lightning-fast and attacking style. North Melbourne, who have won two consecutive AFLW premierships, currently have five Irish players on their list, while the Brisbane Lions, Adelaide, Geelong and Carlton all have a strong contingent of Irish players. Erone Fitzpatrick is one of 46 Irish players in the AFLW. Joe Armao The impact in Ireland has been seismic as well. On one hand, the game’s popularity has surged, with Irish broadcasters showing AFLW games, dedicated 3am watch parties and growing fan bases on social media.

But the amount of Irish-born players lured to Australia has also left a growing hole in Gaelic football pathways, especially in smaller regions, “I’m from a very small county, not saying that I would have been a big fish, but I probably would have been at home,” Fitzpatrick explains. “For my county to lose like someone like me is hard ... because in a small county, talent is very limited compared to the bigger counties that have a huge pool of talent. “Counties like Mayo have six girls playing in the AFLW – that’s a huge chunk of unbelievable talent from one county.” There’s enough Irish talent in AFLW to make a representative game in the mould of State of Origin possible. Fitzpatrick represented Ireland in that match in Sydney, in front of a sellout crowd. Speaking in the lead-up, Fitzpatrick was thrilled to be part of it. “My parents are flying out for the game, which is so important to me, and I’ll also have my aunties, family friends, my grannies’ next door neighbour,” she joked. “I want to make them proud, and I want to make all the young girls proud and know they can chase their dreams and be anything they want in life.” Related Article Analysis
