title: ‘They hid it away’: The DNA test that revealed an Australian cricketer’s family secret
text:
But the true significance of Gaunt’s debut has been shrouded in a family secret for decades, only recently confirmed by DNA testing: Ron Gaunt may well have been Australia’s first Test cricketer of Indigenous heritage.

After moving to Victoria, Gaunt also made his mark in the east, notably as the longtime bowling coach for the Footscray Cricket Club. It was there he set Merv Hughes on the path to a storied career by telling the young all-rounder from Werribee that he was, in fact, a bowler.

“He was quick and used to swing the ball about quite nicely. Especially on the Perth wicket where he used to get a bit of pace and bounce, he was a nasty proposition for a batsman to face. He was certainly a top-rate fast bowler,” Craig told Cricinfo in 2012.

Gaunt’s story was a good one, of a strapping quick bowler with a shock of red hair, who may well have played many more games for Australia had he not been stuck behind the likes of Alan Davidson and Graham McKenzie.

Within a few days, the 23-year-old Gaunt made his debut in Durban, claiming figures of 2-87 in a drawn match under the captaincy of Ian Craig.

In January 1958, a young West Australian fast bowler by the name of Ron Gaunt was flown into South Africa as an injury replacement for the Australian Test team.

Because of its rich wheat farming, York was home to plenty of prosperous families, who shared the land with the Indigenous community.

The municipality of York, about 100 kilometres east of Perth, is WA’s oldest inland town, established in 1831 after being home to the Ballardong Noongar people for thousands of years.

Gaunt’s story also raises a wider question of Australian cricket, and life. How many more gifted athletes of Indigenous heritage have been part of the nation’s story in secret, because of the past strictures of the White Australia policy?

Since then, Ash Gardner, Scott Boland and Brendan Doggett have joined the list of Indigenous Test cricketers. Boland will proudly take the field for Australia in a Test against Bangladesh in Darwin , amidst one of the nation’s largest Indigenous communities, this week.

His debut came a month earlier than the sole women’s Test played by Aunty Faith Thomas at Melbourne’s Junction Oval in February 1958, and decades before Jason Gillespie took the field for Australia in Sydney in 1996.

As the years went by, rumours circulated that the swarthy complexion of some children was down to Spanish ancestry, or even that someone in the family had married a Pacific Island princess. Anything but Indigenous heritage.

The secrecy started around the time of the First World War, when two family members served, including Arthur Gaunt. When he came back from Europe, Arthur listed his mother’s heritage as Maori, the better to receive a gratitude bond of £100 for returned servicemen.

“All this was kept a secret,” says Ron’s nephew, Dudley Gaunt. “There were laws and restrictions, and it just would’ve made their lives difficult. So they hid it away.”

Walter and Matilda raised her eldest son, Arthur, together, but also had other children, including another named Walter. After Walter junior grew up, he married Ruby Morse, and among six children Ron Gaunt was born in York in 1934.

Matilda Gaunt, who was Indigenous, is seated at right. She was Ron Gaunt’s grandmother.

Matilda was, by all accounts, a formidable figure. Local newspaper reports tell of how, aged 16, she took the local publican to court in York over unpaid wages and won the case. She was a landowner, and after having one child with another man, Matilda married Walter Gaunt, a local bricklayer.

In 1872, John Walkinshaw Cowan, whose brother would marry the revered social reformer and politician Edith Cowan, had a child with an unnamed Aboriginal woman. That child, Matilda Cowan, was Ron Gaunt’s grandmother.

“WA was a very harsh place for Aboriginal people,” says Ron’s niece, Jenny Ewell. “I think they wanted to avoid that, and absolutely because of Ron’s cricket.

It is ironic that two of Gaunt’s three Tests were played against Apartheid South African teams – just another reminder of the complexities facing a young man of mixed race in Australia in the 1950s and ’60s.

Gaunt was among the most promising young fast bowlers in the country, with enough of a competitive streak to indulge in a bit of “Bodyline” bowling for WA in 1956. In a game against Queensland, umpire Colley ordered WA captain Ken Meuleman to change the field, and warned Gaunt about his bowling.

When the Gaunt family moved from York to Perth, as Walter’s building business grew, he purchased land and built a house in a suburb called Rivervale, on the eastern bank of the Swan River. Tellingly, Rivervale was the nearest suburb on the outside of the prohibited area, which was only rescinded in 1954 – well after Ron had started playing club cricket.

In the west, a strict policy was introduced in 1927 to ban the Indigenous community from setting foot into the “Native Prohibited Area” that broadly covered the Perth central business district and select suburbs either side of the Swan River. And in Queensland, an Aboriginal fast bowler named Eddie Gilbert was swift enough to knock the bat out of Don Bradman’s hands, but not to play for Australia.

Much had changed in WA, and Australia, between the late 19th century and the 1930s. Intermarriage between whites and Aboriginal people was first discouraged, then virtually outlawed.

Gaunt, by this time nicknamed “Pappy”, would also mentor Tony Dodemaide, and was instrumental in helping the club win its inaugural first-grade premiership in 1980.

“What he did for me was extraordinary. Without him, I would’ve gone down to Footscray and battled away as a middle-order batsman and part-time bowler. If I had said to Ron, ‘You’re kidding yourself, I’m a batsman’, I’d probably still be plugging away in Footscray thirds now...”

“I reckon I bowled three balls and Ron came down and said you don’t bat any more, you’re a bowler. He stood at the top of my mark for two or three years, just talking bowling, theories, sorting batsmen out, a whole gamut of different things.

“I was a middle-order batsman who bowled maybe second or third change and then got down to Footscray and had a talk to the president, the coach, Ken Eastwood was in on the conversation as seconds captain, and Ron Gaunt was there,” Hughes says.

“Ron absolutely loved playing cricket, he lived and breathed the game, and I think it would have just destroyed him had he not been able to play it. So that’s probably where it came from.”

Hughes remembers Gaunt’s skill as a technical coach, plus his ability to still send down beautiful outswing in the nets. But what sticks with him is the older man’s personal touch – sports psychology before it had the name.

“You could talk to him about anything,” Hughes says. “He could pick up on if you were having a bad day or whatever, and that’s the philosophy I take with kids now. You talk to them, and it’s not just about cricket, but about school, are exams coming up? If guys aren’t concentrating on their bowling, you try to get to the bottom of it, and he used to do that beautifully.

”He knew you had the talent and if you weren’t producing at training he’d try to get to the bottom of it. He’d say, ‘Listen, you’re at training, you can leave that behind, and concentrate on your training’.”

Merv Hughes was mentored by Ron Gaunt at Footscray. Getty

Some earthier incentives came when Hughes and Footscray were fighting for their lives in the 1980 first-grade grand final.

“In the first XI grand final I played in my second year at Footscray, there was 10 and 11 batting, and he just said, ‘Right boys, if you can get to double figures here I’ll buy you a slab’,” Hughes remembers. “How hard do you reckon we worked to get those runs?

“If you did well, he was always there for you. It wasn’t him beating his chest, it was just him patting you on the back and saying, ’Well done’.”

Dodemaide, a couple of years younger than Hughes, can recall watching Gaunt bowl, perhaps planting a seed that led an initially front-on bowler to change his action to allow for the away swingers that netted Dodemaide 10 Test caps.

Australian selector Tony Dodemaide (right). Getty Images

“He had the tracksuit on and was clearly well past playing age, but he went in to bowl a few balls and demonstrate what he was talking about, and he had this beautiful side-on jump and action, and it was just so smooth,” says Dodemaide, now an Australian selector. “I thought, ‘Wow, could I ever bowl like this bloke?’

“Having a couple of Test players around the club was just gold for a young kid like me. He only played a handful of Tests, but that was enough as far as we were concerned – to spend any time around someone who’d played at that level of cricket.”

None of Hughes, Dodemaide or even his fellow Footscray Test cricketer Ken Eastwoood had any idea about Gaunt’s heritage.

“I never knew that, but that’s a real feather in his cap,” Hughes says. “Times have changed for the better. I thought I spent a fair bit of time with him, but it was never mentioned. Back then he might’ve been hiding that heritage.”

There is one former teammate, Lindsay James, who has told Dodemaide that Gaunt did indeed know of his Indigenous heritage, and that the pair discussed it quietly, once, long after both had finished playing and coaching.

“I couldn’t imagine him being a fearsome fast bowler,” Dodemaide says. “He had such a gentle demeanour about him, and very generous with his time and experience.”

After retirement, Gaunt moved to the NSW Central Coast to share more time with his children, Karon and Andrew. Gaunt and their mother had divorced when Andrew was two years old.

“Once a year we used to get to see my father around Christmas time for a month, [and] then he’d have to go back to Victoria to work,” Andrew says. “But when I was around 21-22, I went and stayed with him for a few years, and that was good. He was pretty much just like a mate, he spoke like a mate and that’s how we were.

“I came back to Sydney after a couple of years, and we kept in closer contact, and, eventually, he retired up the Central Coast and I went up and stayed there for a while. But work was back here in Sydney. So I was always going up there weekly, pretty much for years.”

Australian Test players Ron Gaunt (left) who played his first Test against South Africa with captain Bob Simpson and Richie Benaud. "The News" and "The Mail"

Sport in general, and cricket in particular, was never far away from the conversation.

“You had no choice on the TV, it was cricket when it started until it finished, then he’d go, ‘OK it’s yours now’,” Andrew recalls. “He never boasted, he never bragged, that wasn’t him. Other people who knew him would say, ‘That’s Ronnie Gaunt, he used to play for Australia’. But he’d never say that. He wouldn’t talk too much about it – what happens on tour stays on tour almost.”

If Gaunt was taciturn about his cricket achievements, his heritage was buried deeper still, remaining unknown to the family when Ron died in 2012. Eight years later, during COVID-19, Andrew’s half-sister Kellie started digging into family history. Ancestry searches were followed by DNA tests, revealing a hidden Indigenous bloodline.

Indigenous Test star Scott Boland. Getty Images

“One day, out of the blue she gave me a call and said, ‘Andrew, guess what, you’ll never believe it’, and I just said, ‘Nah, get out of here’. And my other sister Karon couldn’t believe it at all.

“Then Kellie got in contact with Jenny, and she took it up and ran with it. It was a such a well-kept secret, and maybe that was a reason why. He may not have played for Australia or got the chances he did if they knew he had Indigenous background.

“I was speaking to my sisters about Jason Gillespie saying, ‘Geez, he’s supposed to be the first person of Indigenous blood to play for Australia’. I started laughing about that and going, ‘Oh man, sorry about that’.”

Ask Andrew what he might have said to his father had he known, and he pauses.

“I’d probably have said, ‘What the hell were you thinking?’” he laughs. “I’m actually quite proud or glad, it just cements that footprint in our family as a full-on Aussie. But I don’t think they looked at it like that.”

While Ron got his mother Ruby’s red hair, Andrew and Jenny are both darker in complexion. Andrew can remember, as a teenager, that Ron got them together at Martin Place in Sydney.

“I met Jenny one time when I was about 16,” he says. “Dad was in Melbourne at the time, but he came up to see us. He wanted me to go and meet my cousin, he goes, ‘Come and meet your cousin’, and Karon said, ‘What about me?’ and he says, ‘Nah, just Andrew’. I thought that was a bit odd.

“That’s the first and last time I met Jenny [who moved to the United States, where she still lives]. But I think Dad was sizing me up with her because we were both darker in complexion. That’s just my take, but my sisters Karon and Kellie thought that made sense.”

After Jenny took up the family research, she passed much of the information onto Dudley Gaunt, who still lives in WA. He has had inconclusive discussions with WA Cricket about Ron’s Indigenous heritage, and has also made attempts to contact the Ballardong Noongar community. Cricket Australia is looking into the Gaunt family story.

“We want to ensure cricket’s heritage fully reflects all those from different backgrounds who have contributed to the game,” a CA spokesman said.

“The stories provided by those exploring family ancestry is an important way to ensure the diverse backgrounds of past players is recognised.”

Dudley says the main issue in his meeting with WA Cricket was not Gaunt’s Aboriginality, “It was whether he accepted his Aboriginality, whether he told people. Did he tell people at South Perth cricket club?

“If he wouldn’t have been able to play cricket, why would he tell anyone at South Perth that he was Aboriginal? It was a different time, they parked it away, hid it and got on with their lives.”

In 2005, the former chief justice of NSW, James Spiegelman, spoke about hidden Aboriginal histories in that year’s Charles Perkins Oration.

“Let me state one undeniable fact: many, probably millions of Australians have an Aboriginal ancestor,” he said. “This should be recognised as an important bond. However, most do not know this fact about their family.

“There was a strong sense of racism involved in the suppression in thousands upon thousands of Australian families of the Aboriginal origins of one or more of their forebears. For most of our history this has been regarded as a matter to be suppressed.

“It appears to me that the process of reconciliation would be advanced by a wider recognition across the broad Australian community that the number of Australians who have Aboriginal ancestors probably amounts to millions.

“The reconciliation process cannot succeed if it is based, contrary to historical fact, solely on maintaining a rigid and categorical distinction between black and white. It will succeed if a significant proportion of those Australians of whom it is true take pride in acknowledging their roots in both communities.”

For Jenny, the secret is itself a significant part of the story.

“I was very proud to find that out myself, to think we’ve got heritage that goes back 60,000 years in Australia,” she says. “But in going back to speak to the family, I found out that the family did know, and didn’t say anything.

“I was shocked, thinking, ‘Gosh they kept it a good secret all those years’. But a lot of it might have been that they wanted to work and get on with their lives. This is my opinion – because Ron was playing cricket and very successful, they wanted that to keep going and that it wasn’t made more difficult for him.”

Andrew recalls one other comment from his father that has taken on new meaning.

“My dad used to tell me, ‘You have a whole other family in the west’,” he says. “It was a big secret, and back then I could understand it. Whereas now I’m like, ‘Wow, that’s cool’.”

title: Planes narrowly avoid runway collision as delays continue at Sydney Airport

Passengers departing from Sydney Airport have experienced significant delays, a result of staff shortages.

Two planes have narrowly avoided collision on the tarmac at Sydney Airport, after days of significant delays.

A Jetstar Airbus A320 was entering an intersection at around 7am on Sunday morning when it suddenly braked to avoid being hit by an incoming Qatar Airways Boeing 777 — towed by a tug.

There were no passengers aboard the Qatar plane. However, the Gold Coast-bound Jetstar flight reported the injury of a staff member.

In footage uploaded to social media from inside the Jetstar plane, the pilot can be heard updating the passengers.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who has endured a week of scathing criticism revolving around the now-shelved private investment plan, has been accused by a British newspaper of paying off an alleged lover while at UEFA.

According to The Telegraph, the Italian-Swiss lawyer, who served as secretary general of European football's governing body from 2009 to 2016, also previously used his influence to secure a promotion for the same UEFA employee with whom he was in an intimate relationship.

Infantino has categorically denied the allegations, according to the article, which was published on Saturday.

When contacted by the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency on Saturday, a FIFA spokesperson had not responded.

"But scrutiny is not a licence to distort facts, amplify unsubstantiated allegations or manufacture distractions designed to undermine progress. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading, FIFA will challenge it directly and vigorously," it added.

FIFA said Saturday it "will not support, facilitate or tolerate any process concerning the election of the FIFA President that is inconsistent with FIFA's Statutes, democratic procedures and established governance framework".

title: A diamond is forever, but its rarity isn't: How technology rewrote a billion-year-old story
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Once upon a time, a diamond engagement ring was a powerful symbol of social status: the bigger the rock, the greater its cachet.

Today, ring owners posting in social media forums will often voice a different sentiment: "Does this look too big?"

The diamond industry has undergone an unprecedented shake-up in recent years due to the exploding popularity of lab-grown gems.

The price of a one-carat natural diamond has more than halved since the start of 2022, according to US industry data.

Last month, De Beers — the company that helped define the diamond industry and monopolised it for decades — suspended production at South Africa's biggest diamond mine, citing a need to cut costs amid challenging market conditions.

It's the latest sign that the once-booming industry is at a crossroads as collapsing diamond prices force mining behemoths to close mines, delay new projects and suspend production.

At the heart of the upheaval is a physically identical product that has upended one of the most successful luxury marketing stories ever told.

Lab-grown diamonds are real diamonds — chemically and visually identical to those found deep underground.

But rather than forming inside the Earth over a billion years or more, lab gems are created by scientists using one of two primary methods — High Pressure High Temperature (HPHT) or Chemical Vapour Deposition (CVD) — to recreate the conditions under which carbon crystallises into diamond.

It takes a matter of weeks.

How did the story of a gem forged over billions of years, and sold for generations as a symbol of rarity and exclusivity, change so dramatically in just a decade?

A history of diamond-making

After years of experimentation, the first proven human-made diamonds were created in the 1950s.

At the time, there was little concern that they could become serious competition for natural diamonds.

The early synthetic stones were small, brown and of poor quality for use in jewellery, instead used for industrial purposes such as manufacturing.

It wasn't until the 1970s that General Electric, the American company that pioneered synthetic diamond technology, produced the first gem-quality lab diamonds.

But the technology was still too expensive to make lab diamonds commercially viable for jewellery, and the stones weren't graded highly under gem colour and clarity standards.

A 'diamond seed' is a tiny, microscopic slice of diamond.

As the technology continued to improve, a turning point arrived in 2007: the Gemological Institute of America (GIA), the world's leading independent authority on gem-grade diamonds, officially recognised lab diamonds.

The GIA began issuing reports for lab gems that year, but they represented only a tiny fraction of diamonds submitted for grading — around 0.05 per cent.

A decade later, lab-grown diamonds still only accounted for a small share of the global market.

But in the last few years, they've erupted into the mainstream.

Paul Zimnisky, a leading independent diamond industry analyst based in New York City, says the influx of lab gems has dramatically altered the global market.

"The technology to make those diamonds has rapidly improved, and the price to make them has come down substantially," Zimnisky tells SBS News.

As the price has come down, that's when I've really seen consumer demand pick up for the man-made diamonds, and that I would say happened within the last five years in a big way.

In 2016, a one-carat natural diamond would retail in the US for around $9 , 380, while a lab-grown stone of the same cut and clarity would cost $7 , 820, according to Zimnisky's data.

Today, the natural diamond retails for $4,900 while the equivalent lab stone can be bought for around $850 or less.

Zimnisky estimates lab-grown stones now account for around a third of the global diamond jewellery market.

Credit: Paul Zimnisky data and analysis

In the US, the world's largest consumer market for diamonds, six in 10 engaged couples opted for a lab diamond last year, according to annual survey data from wedding planning website The Knot.

That was a 239 per cent increase from the site's 2020 survey.

At the same time, as lab diamonds are shifting consumer trends, they are also changing global manufacturing and production flows.

With production costs declining, manufacturers in China and India have expanded at an unprecedented scale.

In China, which dominates the global production market, the central province of Henan has become known as the nation's "diamond capital". In the city of Zhecheng's many factories, hundreds of machines work around the clock to produce millions of carats each year.

Today, even experts say they can't distinguish between a natural or lab-grown diamond without specialised equipment.

"The only way to tell the difference is either through the laser inscription, which is usually engraved on the girdle of the diamond, or through a certificate which is associated with the diamond," Michael Cohen, managing director of the Diamond Certification Laboratory of Australia, tells SBS News.

"Other than that, you need to put it to a laboratory to actually know the difference. It's not possible to actually see it visually through a microscope, through basic testing, even your countertop retail test."

But De Beers has been working to change that.

The London-headquartered multinational has developed a suite of advanced screening machines, costing from around $7,900 to more than $35,000, which allow diamond sellers to distinguish between natural and lab-grown diamonds by analysing microscopic signatures left behind by their different growth processes.

The technology forms part of the company's broader effort to persuade consumers that a diamond's origin, rather than its composition, is an important part of its story.

READ MORE Why Australia ships out its wealth — and buys it back as finished goods

The rise of the big diamond

As larger diamonds have become more affordable and visible on social media, demand for smaller stones of one carat or less has slowed.

Designs that were once reserved for celebrities and the ultra-wealthy are now well within reach for many middle-income earners.

And it's not just the price that's more attractive: ethical concerns over the origin of gems have been offset by the lab-grown model, which does not rely on mining or supply chains that pass through conflict zones.

On Reddit forums, it's now common to see everyday people asking whether a diamond looks "too big" or ostentatious on their finger.

At the same time, some owners of natural diamonds have posted on social media worried that people will assume their ring is lab-grown as large diamonds become increasingly prevalent.

It reflects a generational change in consumer sentiment — one that is fast becoming an identity crisis for the natural diamond industry.

De Beers launched its own lab-grown jewellery brand in 2018 but shuttered it last year to focus on its original product.

It has outlined a plan to invest in emotionally driven campaigns that emphasise the rarity and origin of natural diamonds.

Cohen says the company realised it was giving lab-grown diamonds credibility by selling them under the De Beers banner, but its exit did little to slow demand.

Jana Bowden is a professor of marketing and consumer behaviour at Macquarie University, and says much of the identity crisis faced by major brands stems from the historical emphasis on a diamond's exclusivity .

"Diamonds have always been seen as an absolute status symbol," she says.

"So much of this has been driven by the perceived rarity and exclusivity of the diamonds, and of course the controlled supply of diamonds through the market, and particularly De Beers as being the pinnacle brand with the most control of the market and supply."

From rare to abundant: The 'forever' diamond

At its peak in the 1980s, De Beers controlled nearly 90 per cent of the global diamond market.

Its tight control of the world's diamond supply allowed it to stockpile excess diamonds and manage how many entered the market at any time, helping to keep prices elevated.

Through its marketing, the company famously built the idea that a diamond is rare, "forever", and the ultimate expression of love, turning diamond engagement rings into a social norm.

It also molded societal expectations around how much an engagement ring should cost.

"Isn't two months' salary a small price to pay for something that lasts forever?" a 1980s De Beers ad asked.

Bowden says historic luxury brands like De Beers built lasting perceptions in consumers' minds.

Really, we've been taught and we have learnt how to incorporate diamonds into our lives. This is not something that existed prior to the clever marketing campaigns.

Although diamonds are now far from rare, Bowden says many of those perceptions persist — but the market is splitting in two.

"Interestingly, the legacy branding that's come from the original, traditional mining of diamonds is also now naturally transferred to lab diamonds as well. So consumers still have that association with exclusivity or a milestone."

Bowden says the lab-grown diamond market is increasingly appealing to younger consumers, who are often more financially constrained and ethically motivated than older generations.

A three-carat natural diamond (left) and a three-carat lab-grown diamond (right) side by side. Source: Getty / Picture alliance

Ms Elangovan, 33, who asked to omit her first name to protect her privacy, tells SBS News she has accumulated more than 10 lab-grown and natural diamonds in her jewellery collection over the past decade or so.

While she's fascinated by the history and rarity of a natural diamond, she can no longer justify the price when she can buy a "virtually flawless" lab equivalent at a fraction of the price.

"When I look at it, I'm like, 'Oh, this existed millions of years before me, and it probably would [for] millions of years after me," she says of natural diamonds.

"So on that point, labs can't compete."

But ultimately, she says she's thrilled to be living in an age where beautiful jewels are accessible to more people.

"I'm intrigued [that] someone can just recreate millions of years of process in a lab," she says.

"It's a fascinating industry. I'm just happy I'm alive now, so I can have really pretty jewellery at a very affordable price and ethically sourced."

Can the mined diamond industry recover?

The natural diamond industry is now facing headwinds from multiple directions.

Changing consumer spending priorities, skyrocketing operational costs, geopolitical uncertainty, and declining diamond yields have all contributed to mines closing or suspending production in recent years.

Some mines were approaching the end of their lifespan regardless, but plummeting diamond prices and the enormous cost to open new mines have made it harder to justify investment in new projects.

"I think the natural diamond industry has to collect itself and come up with a strategy to further differentiate its product from lab-grown diamonds," Zimnisky says, adding that the industry must give consumers a compelling reason to pay 10 times as much for a natural stone.

He notes that De Beers is currently up for sale by its parent company, Anglo American, with a potential deal expected this year.

The new owner's arrival will be "an interesting catalyst" for the industry, he says.

I think they're probably going to pretty aggressively try to kind of reignite interest and demand and emotional appeal for natural diamonds.

For now, unless prices double or triple over the next decade, Zimnisky doesn't expect to see significant investment in new mines or the reopening of suspended operations.

Cohen, who has worked in the industry for more than 40 years, says there'll now be a "never-ending supply" of lab diamonds. But he expects prices may eventually increase as the significant energy required to produce them becomes more expensive — which could potentially create new ethical concerns for consumers.

He believes diamond mining will eventually come to an end, but the market for natural diamonds will endure.

"The biggest supply of diamonds will no longer come from the mine, but it'll come from the second-hand markets," he says.

"The diamonds don't get destroyed. As they say, a diamond is forever."

title: This tiny NSW town is set to become a $560m US defence 'cornerstone'
text:
in brief The US Pentagon has pledged $566 million for an Australian mine.

This project aims to secure critical defence minerals to counter Chinese supply.

A remote Australian town is set to become a "cornerstone" of the Western supply of scandium, a rare earth mineral needed for defence, planes, and data centres after local mining company Sunrise Energy Metals secured a US$400 million ($566m) pledge.

The Pentagon revealed the details of the conditional loan commitment to Sunrise to build the world's first primary mine for scandium, of which China dominates supply and processing, at a meeting between US President Donald Trump and mining executives in Washington.

Scandium is usually sourced as a byproduct of other mining and is found throughout the Earth's crust in low concentrations.

"We aim to establish Syerston as a cornerstone of Western scandium supply," Sunrise chairman Robert Friedland said in a statement, referring to the proposed mine in Fifield, New South Wales.

Fifield is a remote town in the centre of the state, roughly 450 kilometres west of Sydney. 2016 census data shows just 129 people live in the town that boasts a single pub.

NSW has some of the highest concentrations of scandium globally, Resources Minister Madeline King said.

"The Sunrise scandium project hosts the world's largest and highest-grade known scandium resource, which has a range of vital aerospace, defence and clean energy applications," she said.

"No one country alone can create secure, end-to-end supply chains in critical minerals and rare earths.

"In working together, Australian mining companies can create more jobs and investment opportunities here at home, and more jobs and investment in the United States."

King described the announcement as a "significant vote of confidence" in Australia's capacity to supply the US and its allies with the minerals they need.

China restricted exports of scandium for defence products last year, triggering the US search for new suppliers.

The Pentagon statement said the scandium project will "ensure Western alignment from mine to finished product".

"Secretary Hegseth and Deputy Secretary Feinberg are mobilizing the Department of War's resources to secure our critical mineral supply chain," said Emil Michael, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering.

Trump and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese signed a critical minerals agreement aimed at countering China in October, pledging that each would invest $1 billion in projects.

On Saturday, Trump announced that the US was reclaiming its place as the "minerals superpower of the world."

"Critical minerals are the raw materials of American strength that power everything from advanced weaponry to automobiles, and we want these essential products to be mined, refined and made right here in the USA," he said.

Sunrise struck a deal with Lockheed Martin last year to sell the defence and aerospace manufacturer 25 percent of its scandium output for the first five years of the mine.

The company will make an announcement to the Australian Securities Exchange on Monday, Friedland said.

The mine is set to have an initial capacity of 60 tonnes a year of scandium oxide and will commence production in the first half of 2028.

title: Kmart's Smart Glasses have sold out. Their popularity pushed a national privacy probe
text:
IN BRIEF Meta's AI glasses and cheaper alternatives have sparked rising concerns over privacy.

Australia's Privacy Commissioner will investigate the safety impacts of the wearable technology at the request of the Attorney-General.

The $89 Kmart alternative to Meta's artificial intelligence glasses has sold out. Its popularity has contributed to a government push to investigate privacy protections.

Released on 28 July, Anko's Smart Glasses were cleared from shelves across the country in under a week.

The product offered discreet surveillance technology to the mass market, selling for at least $200 less than premium Meta versions, which have been available for years.

The black-rimmed, clear-lens glasses can record high-definition video and snap photographs, which are then quickly transfered to smartphones.

Using HeyCyan software, users can also answer calls, listen to music and use an AI assistant.

Kmart is among many retailers, including Amazon, Temu and AliExpress, that are selling cheaper alternatives.

On Friday, the Attorney-General, Michelle Rowland, appealed to Australia's Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) to investigate the potential privacy implications of smart glasses.

Rowland requested that the independent statutory agency give the issue priority consideration, citing serious safety concerns for women and children.

"Privacy is an essential part of all our lives; it allows us to be who we are with dignity and without fear," Rowland said.

Kmart's $89 smart glasses have sold out online within one week. Credit: Kmart.com.au

"Unlike other forms of technology, smart glasses may be used more discreetly, making it harder to know when you are being recorded.

"The OAIC regularly monitors the effects of new technologies on privacy — and the government has every faith that they will identify any new privacy risks and mitigation measures."

Rowland said the government will also continue to contribute to work to ensure "privacy laws are fit for purpose in the digital age".

According to Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind, 85 per cent of Australians have become increasingly concerned about their personal privacy since 2021.

She said that protections under the Privacy Act don't extend to those filmed by smart glasses and that new laws must be considered.

"Australia’s Privacy Act only applies to businesses and government agencies, not to individuals, and it only applies when those entities collect personal information," Kind wrote in a post to the OAIC webpage.

“In circumstances where a tech company is receiving and storing personal information collected by surveillance wearables, they’ll have to make sure they’re complying with privacy law."

However, she questioned the company's capacity to notify individuals that they are being recorded.

A growing, international concern

The technology has caused a stir worldwide, with some already taking steps to limit use. In the United Kingdom, they are restricted in a string of hospitality and entertainment venues.

Jeremy King, owner of multiple popular hospitality venues in London, said guests would be expected to remove smart glasses while dining in his venues.

"I would never knowingly allow any invasion of guest privacy other than the eyes we were born with," he told The Guardian.

Popular pub chain Wetherspoons also won't allow the glasses.

"The general code that applies in our pubs, and most pubs, is that you can't film customers or employees without their permission," said chief executive Tim Martin.

"Meta glasses seem to breach this code, and common sense, by enabling surreptitious surveillance, so our instinct is to say turn off the cameras," he told The Guardian.

ATG Theatres, which operates Bristol Hippodrome, Edinburgh Playhouse and other esteemed theatres across London, also said they would not allow guests to wear the glasses during performances.

title: House prices are falling, but first home buyers like Grace say corrections haven't helped
text:
IN BRIEF Repeated RBA rate hikes have slashed the borrowing power of individual Australians by $35,400.

The housing market is expected to continue its trend downward with capital cities falling 5 per cent across 2026.

House prices are falling. But for Grace, buying her first home still comes with compromise.

The 29-year-old Wollongong resident and her partner began searching for their home earlier this year, conveniently as the market began trending down.

"It just happened to happen when I was ready to start looking," the 29-year-old told SBS News.

"We went into it pretty open-minded as we didn't know what we'd be able to afford, but heard prices may be dropping with the tax changes."

The pair had hoped to buy in the city where they live on NSW's south coast — but it's beyond their budget.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We're looking to buy south where prices are more within range," she said.

She said it was a "compromise" on what they wanted.

While the slump has made the market more attractive, Grace said there are still major issues.

"While the first home buyer scheme makes it more accessible to purchase a home, massive mortgage repayments are still a huge barrier, so I'll only buy somewhere where I can put down at least a 10 per cent deposit," she said.

"Another barrier is definitely bidding against those with clearly more money than you from the bank of mum and dad".

Borrowing power slashed

Money may be on the mind of many potential buyers, with new data reporting a significant drop in borrowing power since the start of 2026, thanks to the three consecutive Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) interest rate hikes seen so far this year.

New data from Canstar reveals that an average income earner's maximum borrowing capacity had fallen by an estimated $35,400 since January, while couples seeking to buy a property had theirs slashed by $70,700.

The February RBA interest rate hike dropped borrowing capacity by $12,200 for individuals and $24,400 for couples.

The March hike saw a drop of $11,800 and $23,600, and May's $11,400 and $22,700.

The RBA is expected to hold the cash rate at its next meeting on Tuesday. However, if Australians are subject to another rate hike, borrowing power would drop to $46,300 per person and $92,500 per couple.

READ MORE Home prices fall across Australia as housing downturn takes hold

Canstar's data insights director, Sally Tindall, said it's a "classic case of one step forward and one step back" for prospective buyers.

"While falling property prices may look like a win for people trying to get into the market, higher interest rates are keeping borrowing budgets in a bind," she said.

“The challenge for buyers is that a cheaper price tag doesn’t necessarily mean a more affordable home if your borrowing capacity has been cut at the same time."

She said another interest rate increase will "tighten the screws even further".

“Headline inflation might have made a somewhat unexpected drop in June, but core inflation is still sticky," she said.

"The RBA might not hike on Tuesday, but it's difficult to see it ruling out further hikes altogether.

Many first home buyers have been priced out of Sydney, extending their search to Wollongong and beyond. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

Australia's housing market has been experiencing a slump since June, and shows no signs of a plateau.

On Tuesday, NAB released its August Housing Monitor, which predicted that house prices across all major cities will continue to fall.

Melbourne and Sydney median property prices are sitting 5.3 per cent and 5.1 per cent below recent peaks, while Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide are 0.4 to 0.7 per cent lower.

NAB forecast that property prices across all capital cities could fall collectively by 5 per cent across 2026.

Sydney alone is expected to experience a total drop of up to 10 per cent — with the median house price in Sydney estimated at $1,452,024 by December, dropping $160,000 over the year.

Brisbane prices could drop $28,380 by December and Perth and Adelaide by $17,200 and $30,754 respectively.

By December, the cheapest capital city to buy a property in will be Hobart, at $807,260.

NAB also predicted the market will make a small "recovery" in late 2027.

“NAB’s latest revised forecast points to further softening in property prices through to the end of the year, not just in Sydney and Melbourne but in other capitals that were previously defying the rate hikes," said Tindall.

She said it's a "tough pill to swallow" for homeowners who purchased their home during the peak with "next to no buffer".

"Negative equity is a very real prospect for these borrowers. The key is to run your own race," Tindall said.

“As a potential new buyer, make sure you have plenty in the tank in case of tougher times ahead. Existing borrowers should prepare for another hike, even if the headlines are suggesting we’re already at the peak.

"Certainly, the RBA has not declared the battle with inflation won and done.”

title: US-styled large trucks linked to a higher risk of pedestrian deaths, Australian study finds
text:
In brief Australian study links larger utes and US-style trucks to a much higher pedestrian death risk.

Researchers say growing vehicle size may be driving rising pedestrian fatalities nationwide.

For several years now, more Australians have been dying on the road.

This trend is moving Australia further away from its Vision Zero ambition — a national commitment to eliminate all road deaths and serious injuries by 2050.

But what is driving the increase? And is the trend evenly distributed across different road users?

The answer to the first question is complex. The short answer to the second is no.

A bucked trend

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Historical data show that for much of the past two decades, population-adjusted fatality rates for pedestrians and car occupants (drivers and passengers) broadly followed the same downward trajectory.

But since 2021, the two trends have started to noticeably diverge. Pedestrian fatality rates have been rising, while those for drivers and passengers have remained relatively stable.

Does this indicate some systemic change in our road system? We know vehicles on Australian roads are getting progressively bigger: more protective of their own occupants, but potentially more dangerous to those outside them.

Could that explain this divergence, at least in part?

To find out, we conducted the first Australian study to investigate this question using detailed pedestrian crash data.

We linked each crash to the size and weight of the vehicle involved and developed statistical models to isolate the contribution of vehicle size while accounting for other important factors.

The changing shape of Australia’s cars

Data show the average footprint (the ground area covered by the car) of light vehicles in Australia has increased by around 7% since 2005.

For utes and US-style trucks, the increase has been even greater, approaching 18%.

This means the gap between conventional passenger cars and utes/US-style pick-up trucks continues to widen.

There are also more bigger cars on our roads. In 2012, of all new vehicles sold in Australia, only about one quarter were SUVs. By 2023, they accounted for 57%.

This transformation is reflected in the crash data too. Between 2012 and 2024, the average weight of passenger vehicles involved in pedestrian crashes in Victoria rose from about 1,440 kilograms to 1,570 kg – an increase of around 130 kg (9%).

Does bigger mean deadlier?

For years, evidence that larger passenger vehicles are more dangerous to pedestrians has come almost entirely from the United States.

We wanted to know whether the same relationship exists in Australia.

To answer that question, we analysed 10,376 pedestrian crashes involving passenger vehicles in Victoria between 2012 and mid-2025. Heavy vehicles such as trucks and buses were excluded.

The crash records contained detailed information on the circumstances of every collision, including the road environment, speed limit, driver and pedestrian characteristics, time of day and other factors.

We then linked every crash to the weight and height of the vehicle involved by matching its make, model and year with external vehicle specification databases.

We then built statistical models to isolate the contribution of vehicle size while accounting for the other factors that influence pedestrian survival. In other words: if two otherwise similar pedestrian crashes differed only in the size of the vehicle involved, how much would that change the likelihood of a fatal outcome?

Here’s what we found:

every additional 100 kg of vehicle weight was associated with a 6% increase in the odds of pedestrian fatality

every additional 10 cm of height was associated with an 11% increase in the odds of pedestrian fatality

utes and US-style pick-up trucks were associated with around 60% higher pedestrian fatality risk than conventional passenger cars

the relationship was even stronger in lower-speed environments.

We then simulated a scenario in which the larger vehicles involved in these crashes were hypothetically reduced to the size of a typical passenger vehicle today, while everything else about the crashes stayed the same.

The model predicted about 9% fewer pedestrian fatalities.

We also tested the reverse scenario by hypothetically increasing the weight and height of the vehicles involved. As expected, the likelihood of pedestrian death increased – but the rise was consistently greater for height than for weight.

In other words, pedestrian fatality risk appeared more sensitive to increases in vehicle height.

This is largely because taller vehicles are more likely to impact people’s upper body, chest or head.

What does this mean?

Our evidence now suggests, much like in the US, larger passenger vehicles are associated with more severe outcomes for pedestrians in Australia, too.

The difference is Australia appears to be earlier in this transition.

Without policy change, that transition is likely to continue, just as it has done in the US in the past decade.

What can be done?

In Australia, many larger vehicles attract favourable tax treatments, while manufacturers aggressively promote them.

Then there is the belief that bigger means safer. This is a key ingredient car manufacturers use to promote bigger cars, and is believed to be the main driver of the car size race.

Governments at all levels have a range of policy levers they can use to nudge things in a safer and more sustainable direction.

Possible options are:

removing tax concessions that favour larger passenger vehicles

making vehicle purchase taxes or registration fees proportional to vehicle weight or size

introducing additional licensing requirements for the largest passenger vehicles, including restrictions for probationary licence holders

making parking charges or even road penalties proportional to vehicle size.

The early warning signs are clear and, without meaningful policy change, this trend is unlikely to reverse. Governments at every level could have a role to play in changing its course.

title: 'No consultations': Pacific communities shocked by controversial US auction proposal
text:
In brief A US proposal to carve up sections of sea floor close to some Pacific nations has generated controvsery.

Pacific territories controlled by the US have expressed dismay, saying they were not told of the proposal.

A Pacific island leader says there were "no consultations" before the US announced swathes of nearby ocean could be auctioned for deep-sea mining exploration, telling the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency the industry faced strong opposition among his people.

Commonwealth of Northern Mariana Islands Governor David Apatang said the idea had caused great unease across the tropical island chain of some 40,000 people.

The United States alarmed its tropical island territories earlier this year, detailing plans to carve up parts of the Pacific Ocean for mining exploration.

Mining companies see enormous wealth in mineral deposits scattered across the seabed, but the fledgling industry has for years been held back by environmental concerns.

An expanse of US maritime territory near American Samoa in the South Pacific could be auctioned as soon as November, according to official documents.

Separate tracts of ocean surrounding Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands in the Western Pacific are also under consideration.

"Some concerns include disruption to food security for the people of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, who rely on the ocean resources for their survival," Apatang told AFP.

Washington initially proposed to explore a 140,000 square kilometre block about 200 kilometres east of the territory's capital Saipan.

But Apatang said he was caught by surprise when the US announced in March that a similar-sized block to Saipan's west could be leased as well.

"There have been no consultations with the people of the Northern Mariana Islands," he said.

Deep-sea mining companies want to scour the ocean's abyssal plains for mineral deposits and polymetallic nodules laden with nickel, copper and cobalt.

'Unleashing' resources

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order in 2025 aimed at "unleashing" these seabed resources, stressing the demand in everything from renewable energy to military applications.

Critics fear deep-sea mining will cause irreversible damage, smothering marine life in plumes of waste and disrupting oceanic migrations with the thrum of heavy machinery.

The Mariana Islands, Guam and American Samoa all want at least a temporary ban on deep-sea mining in their territorial waters.

But the US territories — which rely on Washington DC for funding and defence — have little say on what it does outside their 5km maritime boundary.

Guam passed laws this year banning deep-sea mining vessels from calling at its ports, potentially hampering the industry by cutting off a crucial source of fuel and supplies.

Apatang said the Northern Mariana Islands would "consider following suit".

Plans for deep-sea mining exploration are most advanced for a vast sweep of ocean near American Samoa, a US territory nestled between New Zealand and Hawaii in the South Pacific.

The US Bureau of Ocean Energy Management is proposing to hold an auction in November, selling exploration licenses for a 125,000 square kilometre block.

The area borders the vast Rose Atoll marine sanctuary, where endangered species of Hawksbill turtle thrive on vibrant reefs.

Lawmaker Aumua Amata, who represents American Samoa in the US House of Representatives, said she worried deep-sea mining could disrupt fisheries providing the vast bulk of the territory's export earnings.

"I represent our people, and I am confident that a majority of American Samoans are opposed," she told AFP.

The licenses cover preliminary surveys and sampling, with future decisions on commercial exploitation needing further bureau approval.

Money for 'nothing'

American Samoa-based environmental advocate Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka said it was impossible to put a "price tag" on the ocean.

"It's not something you think: 'How much money can you make off it?'."

Former US diplomat Emily Wood has been working with the Guam governor's office to better understand the risks of deep-sea mining.

She said leading mining company Impossible Metals had pledged to share one percent of profits with island communities.

"That's nothing at all, compared to the potential damage they might cause," she told AFP.

Impossible Metals did not reply to a request for comment.

The company has previously stated it will not start mining until it is satisfied it is safe.

Pacific island nations are divided on whether deep-sea mining will deliver economic windfalls, or environmental catastrophe.

Nauru and the Cook Islands are among world leaders in seabed mining exploration, while the likes of Samoa, Fiji and Palau have called for a moratorium on the industry.

The US Bureau of Ocean Energy Management was approached for comment.

title: Infantino wins key backing as pressure over FIFA turmoil refuses to fade
text:
In brief FIFA president Gianni Infantino was supported by African and some American confederations.

By contrast, the Norwegian federation called for Infantino's immediate resignation, signalling his leadership crisis is not yet over.

Beleaguered FIFA president Gianni Infantino has received some much-needed support after over a week of scathing criticism revolving around the now-shelved private investment plan, but there was again a call Saturday for him to resign.

The 56-year-old Italian-Swiss lawyer's position remains far from assured despite support from friends he has made during his 10 years in power, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and leading figures in South American football.

FIFA said it could raise up to US$4.2 billion based on a valuation of US$20 billion for a new commercial subsidiary, called the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which it proposed would run events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.

However, old ties have been cut loose.

European football's governing body, UEFA, which he served as secretary-general from 2009-16, is in open conflict with FIFA and on Thursday doubled down on last Saturday's statement, saying it no longer has "confidence" in Infantino.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

UEFA repeated its threat of boycotting the World Cups and one of its member associations, the Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) called for Infantino to go immediately.

"We (NFF) are going to ask the FIFA president to resign now," said its straight-talking president Lise Klaveness on Friday.

Infantino is nigh on certain not to heed such a call and carry on his campaign to be elected for a fourth and final term in Rabat next March.

Infantino, who had spent the past turbulent week amongst friends in Morocco who are co-hosting the 2030 World Cup, is for the moment the only candidate.

The deadline for nominations is 18 November.

There is also a mechanism whereby an extraordinary FIFA congress can be called and a vote of no confidence in Infantino held.

Klaveness, also a lawyer, would be many people's choice as a successor, and also the first woman to be head of world football.

READ MORE FIFA abandons World Cup privatisation plan after fierce backlash

However, Klaveness told AFP her personal ambitions had not played a role in demanding Infantino's resignation.

"We're not there yet," said Klaveness.

"For us, it's now about the issues I just mentioned, and not about particular individuals.

"It would be strange for me to start answering questions about myself, and that goes for everyone," the 45-year-old added.

'Public lynching'

North and Central America's governing body CONCACAF's president Victor Montagliani has been the most oft-cited name in terms of challenging Infantino.

CONCACAF — which includes the three co-hosts of the recent World Cup — had been, along with UEFA, the most brutal in their criticism of Infantino and called for "a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency".

However, there has been radio silence from CONCACAF since the latest FIFA statement backing Infantino was issued on Thursday following an emergency meeting of senior directors in Morocco.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) had also been critical of the manner in which the plan had been handled but, like CONCACAF, kept its own counsel following the FIFA statement.

However, Infantino, who has moved on to Colombia where he attended Friday's inauguration of the country's hard-right president Abelardo de la Espriella in Cali, is not without support.

Photos released by the Colombian Football Federation show a smiling Infantino standing alongside South American Football Confederation (CONMEBOL) president Alejandro Dominguez and the president of the Colombian federation, Ramon Jesurun.

CONMEBOL, which includes iconic federations such as Argentina and Brazil, had on Thursday expressed its "concern regarding the repeated unilateral actions taken" by FIFA.

However, on Friday, the CONMEBOL president told journalists "one cannot ignore the great work" done by Infantino.

"We must continue working for football through dialogue; it is not necessary to always agree," Dominguez added.

Following the powerful Argentine Football Association (AFA) and the Paraguayan federation on Thursday, Infantino also received support Friday from the federations of Venezuela and Ecuador.

Mexico — one of the World Cup co-hosts — also swung behind him.

"The FMF (Mexican Football Federation) supports president Infantino's leadership," it said in a statement.

CAF's executive committee "unanimously reconfirmed its support" for the FIFA president in a statement on Thursday.

The body's decision will have pleased South Africa's sports minister Gayton McKenzie, who had urged African football to resist what he called the "public lynching" of Infantino.

title: AI escaped its testing sandbox and hacked a website. The law is still catching up
text:
In brief A rogue AI model hacked a website. The race to determine who is at fault is underway.

The law is moving to catch up with the rapidly evolving AI space.

Cyberattacks carried out by two OpenAI artificial intelligence models acting autonomously raise a novel legal question: who is responsible when AI goes rogue?

In mid-July, two OpenAI models undergoing testing left their confined environment — a scenario the developers had not anticipated — and ventured out onto the internet, attacking Hugging Face, an AI model-hosting platform.

Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue said Friday his company would not be pursuing legal action at this time.

He added Sunday that the US legal code has to be amended to address such groundbreaking incursions.

"We don't want to end up in a world where everyone is facing cyberattacks all the time because of agents and companies that are creating these agents," Delangue said on CBS News show "Face the Nation."

"So I think it's important for regulators, for policymakers to think about the legal framework of this new kind of technology risk," he added.

In his remarks on Friday, he also mentioned Anthropic, which revealed that three of its models had broken into three different websites, also during testing.

Negligence route

Under US civil and criminal law, unauthorised access to a computer system is an offence.

"If a human OpenAI employee had broken into Hugging Face's systems ... OpenAI would be liable for the employee's wrongful conduct," University of Houston law professor Gabriel Weil wrote in an opinion piece for the Transformer newsletter.

"When an AI agent does it, the law treats it very differently, at least for now," he added.

Matthew Tokson, a University of Utah law professor who focuses on new technologies, had a similar view, saying "we haven't had to grapple with that being formed in anything that's not human, and I don't think courts are likely to be there yet."

The question remains open, however, when it comes to the company that created the model.

"Does 'we didn't tell the AI to do that' end the liability question?" asked Rob T. Lee, head of research at the SANS cybersecurity training institute, in a post on X.

University of Washington law professor Ryan Calo does not believe a criminal case would be likely to succeed.

"The company or individual would have to be at least reckless," he said, explaining they would "be substantially certain the crime would occur and build or prompt the system anyway."

Experts see greater potential for a civil — rather than criminal — case, where the burden of proof is lower.

"Some people think that AI companies should be strictly liable if an AI agent that they deploy totally breaks out, causes damages," Tokson explained.

"Others would prefer to do like a negligence assessment and see if they were actually negligent or if this was just sort of an unavoidable accident or something that couldn't possibly have been foreseen," he added.

In such cases there is a standard of care in product design that judges or juries can use to make a ruling, Tokson continued.

"It's all a bit unwritten because we've never had an AI agent break out of its sandbox and hack other people on the internet before," he said.

OpenAI could rely on the lack of legal precedent if it faced a lawsuit, but those that follow will no longer be able to do so, Calo warned.

Proving that a similar incident could have been anticipated "shouldn't be so hard now that it's begun to happen."

title: For multicultural communities, the Census is about more than population statistics
text:
IN BRIEF Census data informs the funding, access, design and distribution of services for a changing Australia.

When inaccurate or incomplete data is recorded, experts believe there can be serious and sometimes life-threatening consequences.

In 2019, 32-year-old Gia Lam gave birth to a baby boy. Three days later, she was found dead inside her home.

Lam's death was deemed "preventable", according to an inquest released in March by the Coroners Court of NSW. It determined she died from a sepsis infection caused by "multiple failures to diagnose a urinary tract infection".

She was raised in Vietnam and immigrated to Australia around 2010. During her time in hospital, Vietnamese interpreters were not available "during some circumstances", according to the coroner's report.

Priyanka Rai, the executive director of the Australian Multicultural Health Collaborative, said that she has heard of "thousands of stories similar to this".

"In that really, really heartbreaking situation, Gia ... tried to communicate with health services that she was in pain. But there was a gap in that communication, essentially," Rai told SBS News.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"She had a visit by a midwife who did note that she could smell something was off, but she put that down to hygiene, rather than actually trying to look for a clinical cause."

Rai said decisions regarding the funding, availability and allocation of translating and interpreting services — including in healthcare — are informed by the Census of Population and Housing.

The upcoming Census will be held on Tuesday 11 August. The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) will collect data on a person's ancestry, country of birth and whether a language other than English is used at home.

What is the Census?

According to 2021 Census data, an estimated 27.6 per cent of Australians were born overseas, and 48.2 per cent of Australians have a parent born overseas.

Emily Walter is a Census national spokesperson at the ABS and admits that "the Census asks lots of questions" about an individual or household.

But Walter told SBS Hindi that the survey is about "understanding who people are, their cultural background, information about their health and their education and their work status".

"It's all really important information for understanding the community's needs."

Libraries also use information from the Census to build their bilingual book collection and source language support materials. Source: AAP / Sipa USA

Abbas Raza Alvi is the president of the Indian Crescent Society of Australia. He told SBS Hindi that he believes the Census form is "quite complex".

It has up to 66 questions and "sometimes contains words in English that some people find hard to understand", Alvi said.

Online information about the Census is available in 26 languages. People who speak a language other than English can also contact the free Translating and Interpreting Service, which provides access to interpreters who speak more than 150 languages.

How does Census data inform multicultural services?

Census data is used to inform decisions about language services, settlement support, transport, school catchment areas, health care, infrastructure, and business. It also maps and tracks the locations of various populations and key demographics.

This year, the Census will include two new optional questions (for respondents aged 16 or older) about a person's gender identity and sexual orientation. That will be used to determine services for LGBTQI+ populations in Australia.

SBS broadcasts and publishes across more than 60 languages, using data from the Census to ensure its audio, digital, and television offerings reflect the country's evolving demographics.

Researchers rely on Census data too. It's used to study a range of topics including population demographics, economic trends and social issues.

Peter Doukas, chair of the Federation of Ethnic Communities' Council of Australia, told SBS News it's important to ensure "that we can collect accurate demographic data about what makes up Australia".

"That will include things like the kind of languages that are spoken at home and the contraction of some of the more legacy communities."

What community leaders want changed

Question 17 of the Census asks where a person was born.

Countries listed on the Census form include Australia, England, India, New Zealand, the Philippines, Vietnam and South Africa. If a person is born in another country, they can specify this in the 'Other' field.

An ABS spokesperson told SBS Chinese that "the countries listed are the most commonly reported countries of birth in the 2021 Census".

According to 2025 ABS data, an estimated 732,000 people in Australia were born in China. That's an increase of 32,000 compared to 2024 statistics.

However, the spokesperson said China will not be listed as a separate response category.

"This is to encourage people to write in China, Hong Kong, Macau or Taiwan in the 'Other (specify)' box."

Census data is used to plan for infrastructure and services such as schools, hospitals, and social support systems. Source: Getty / AsiaPac

Rai said she believes a question about English proficiency should be added to the Census.

"We need more granular data around not just country of birth, but English proficiency ... that's an important metric of defining what multiculturalism means.

"In health systems, we have data, for instance, in Western Sydney, we do have a large population that was born overseas. But we don't know what their level of English proficiency is."

She said that impacts funding for services, including hospital interpreters.

"It's those experiences of feeling like nobody understands what you're saying and your concerns are dismissed, [that] then feed into these ongoing issues where we already know multicultural communities don't engage with preventative health, often have worse outcomes because they appear later.

"We can see why, because accessing care is so difficult."

title: Beyond money and ambition: Meet the young people defining success differently
text:
The future was everywhere at this year's Garma Festival — in the conversations between young leaders, in the children who eagerly reached for the microphone between interviews, and in the questions about what comes next.

Across four days on Gulkula — an ancient ceremonial site on Gumatj Country in north-east Arnhem Land — the sounds of dance, song and conversation moved through the stringybark forests as young Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander leaders yarned about university degrees, businesses, diplomacy, culture and community leadership.

They voiced ambition without hesitation. But when asked what success means, their answers went beyond careers and salaries.

Instead, they spoke of family. Of culture. Of language. Of Elders. Of Country.

As children gathered nearby, watching the conversation unfold, Ann-Marie Long, a Badjala, Woppaburra and Torres Strait Islander woman and co-founder of Sandpoppy Weaving at First Nations-led organisation EPIC Pathways, reflected on what the notion means to her.
