Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Success for us is about self-determination, being our authentic selves and in a way that we can celebrate, honour and bring many of our community to the table," she tells SBS News.

When I win, my family wins.

But these personal reflections also raise a broader question: how do we measure progress when success is shaped by more than education, employment, and economic opportunity?

National conversations about improving outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people have often focused on measures such as education, employment and economic participation, with a particular emphasis on youth.

For Ann-Marie Long, success is not something achieved alone. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

Under the National Agreement on Closing the Gap, one target aims to increase the proportion of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people aged 15 to 24 who are engaged in employment, education or training to 67 per cent by 2031. In 2021, the figure was 58 per cent.

The agreement also recognises the importance of culture, language, connection to Country and social and emotional wellbeing.

For the young people SBS News spoke with at Garma, these are not separate measures of success; they are part of the same story.

Success rooted in Country

Away from the stages and crowds at Garma, young people connect through movement, storytelling and learning — ancient practices that inform identity and culture.

For Joshua Yow Yeh, dance in particular has become a pathway back to his heritage.

The 20-year-old Yugambeh, Bundjalung, Minjungbal, Bayali, Kabi Kabi and Gooreng Gooreng man is a student at the National Aboriginal and Islander Skills Development Association (NAISDA) dance college. He says it's a space where he can develop his craft while reconnecting with culture and learning from Elders, both of which are key to his notion of success.

It's one he's still learning to define for himself.

"I think I'm coming into success. I'm finding success being here at Garma and being at NAISDA. I think that's what I've defined success as, learning culture, getting knowledge from your Elders, and, you know, finding your family and all that kind of stuff," he tells SBS News.

For Joshua Yow Yeh, success has been found through learning culture, building confidence and carrying knowledge forward. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

Nearby dancers sit on the muddy grounds in groups of two or three, adorned in white ochre, some having just performed, while others prepare for what's ahead.

Watching the movement around him, Yow Yeh speaks about the role creativity could play in shaping his future, not only in terms of his career, but as a way to give back to the community.

"I definitely want to be at home back in my Country in Queensland, surrounded by all my community or my mob learning and then also passing on knowledge, passing on culture, tradition, sharing it with everyone," he says.

Pursuing opportunities away from home is part of the journey, but Yow Yeh's connection to Country remains central to his view of success.

It's a perspective that resonates with 24-year-old Meriki Moran, a Biripi, Dunghutti and Gumbaynggirr man and diploma student at NAISDA.

As Garma wound down, people began packing up around him — loading cars and gathering belongings to leave Gulkula.

The movement around the festival grounds reflected a reality familiar to many young First Nations people: pursuing opportunities can mean leaving home, even temporarily, while finding ways to remain connected to where they come from.

Moran describes that transition as difficult.

"Moving away from your family, moving away from the people that you grew up with that you've known most of your life, to a whole new area with a whole new type of people that are around you. You don't know what's going to happen," he tells SBS News.

Meriki Moran hopes to take the knowledge he has gained from Elders and cultural experiences and bring it back to his community. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

But despite the challenges, Moran says he is driven by a deeper calling: to bring the knowledge and wisdom gained through his experiences back to his community

We are strong when we are together. We are strong when we know everything that we need to know about our culture, our language.

"Success to me looks like moving back home, back to Country, taking in whatever I've learnt from Elders from on Country, any knowledge sharing that's being handed down to me and hopefully taking it back home so I can help teach the next generation," Moran says.

For Asha Bhat, CEO of Southern Aboriginal Corporation, that nexus between personal and collective achievement is something she has witnessed through 18 years of working with Aboriginal communities across regional Western Australia.

Asha Bhat, CEO of Southern Aboriginal Corporation, says many young First Nations people she works with do not define success solely by qualifications, employment, or income. Credit: Supplied

She says many young people she works with do not define success only through qualifications, employment or income.

"It is about knowing who they are, staying connected to their culture and Country, supporting their families, and creating a better future for the next generation," Bhat tells SBS News.

Success does not happen in isolation; instead, cultural connection provides a foundation from which young people can pursue education, employment, and leadership opportunities.

Culture is not separate from success. It is often the reason success becomes possible.

Defining 'wealth' beyond norms

For Tianie Scott-Knight, a Yankunytjatjara, Pitjantjatjara, Anmatyerre, Kamilaroi and Wiradjuri woman, success has meant building a career while staying connected to the cultural foundations that shaped her.

She works as the First Nations public diplomacy lead at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and is currently on leave while studying at NAISDA. The 12-month program has given her an opportunity to reconnect with dance while following in the footsteps of her grandmother, Dorethea Randall, who was among NAISDA's first students in 1976.

Tianie Scott-Knight says the understanding of who you are and where you come from is the foundation of success. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

She says success begins with knowing who you are and where you come from.

I think success to me is being connected to your culture, knowing who you are and who your family is and being proud in that, and just owning your truth.

Like Yow Yeh, Scott-Knight has kept her connection to Country and her communities close, while pursuing opportunities away from home. She says her future aspirations include both professional leadership and creating opportunities for younger generations.

"I think I would be, hopefully, one day a First Nations ambassador. [I] have long-term goals to be in that position, but also I would love to see myself in a community role ... uplifting my community and young ones and inspiring them," she tells SBS News.

Her experience reflects the pathways many young First Nations people are navigating — moving through universities, workplaces and institutions while maintaining connections to family, culture and Country.

Professor Chelsea Watego, a Munanjahli and South Sea Islander woman and executive director of Queensland University of Technology's (QUT) Carumba Institute, has spent more than two decades working across Indigenous research and community-focused initiatives.

She says greater access to education and employment opportunities should not be interpreted as a move away from culture or community.

It should not automatically be assumed that access equates with forgetting who we are and where we come from, or set ourselves apart from our people.

Culture is central to how many First Nations people approach their creative, academic and workplace pursuits.

Eastern Arrernte woman Tanika Anne Orr, owner of Nooks and Cooks bush food catering service, says culture has fundamentally shaped how she approaches her business.

After moving away from Country as a teenager, the now-35-year-old says forging Nooks and Cooks on Kabi Kabi Country on the Sunshine Coast became a way to reconnect with culture while building opportunities with community.

For Tanika Anne Orr, culture has also shaped the way she approaches her bush food catering business. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

"For me, it's not about being successful with money. I think for me, it's more about being successful in having that wealth around you in the way of love and connection," Orr tells SBS News.

Through her business, she hopes to share cultural knowledge and create opportunities for others.

"I really hope that my bush foods business is taking off and is employing a lot of our community."

Carrying Country wherever they go

For many young First Nations people, pursuing education, careers and leadership opportunities can involve moving between communities, cities and regions.

According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, around 15 per cent of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people live in remote or very remote areas, where distance can shape access to services, education and employment opportunities.

On Gumatj Country, surrounded by the sounds and movement of Garma, young people spoke about these choices as part of their journeys — not as leaving one world behind, but as carrying who they are into new spaces.

Long, who runs Sandpoppy Weaving, moved away from home at 17 to study at QUT. While she remained relatively close to Country during her studies, she says she still felt the distance.

"Moving away as a young person definitely had its challenges, but bear in mind, I was only two hours away. I can only imagine the incredible sacrifices that many of our young people from remote and regional communities have to make," she says.

At the same time, the experience also allowed her to explore new ways First Nations stories could be shared and magnified.

It was also really amazing to see the opportunities within the metropolitan areas and the ways that our stories could be told and amplified.

Long says her decisions about education, work and future opportunities are also shaped by family and ancestors. She reflects on the significance of accessing pathways that were not available to previous generations.

"My Nana was a member of the Stolen Generation. So the fact that I can be first in family to go through to Year 10 — let alone to university and pursuing my own business — that incredible privilege is not lost on me."

A similar balancing act has shaped the journey of Willhelm Lauenstein, a Wuthathi man and Indigenous liaison officer for Royal Australian Air Force bases in Darwin and Curtin, critical northern defence facilities for the country.

While carefully painting a yidaki, a traditional Yolŋu instrument also widely known as the didgeridoo, the 32-year-old reflects on the places he has called home.

Willhelm Lauenstein says while living away from home has been challenging, connections can also be built in new places. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

After beginning his career as an electrician and later joining the Air Force, Lauenstein has lived away from his home in Cairns, including time in Katherine and Darwin.

While distance from family has been challenging, he says, connection can also be built in new places.

"I've got no family here. But now I do. Now that I've been here and [in] community and been out and amongst it all, it's like home, second home," Lauenstein tells SBS News.

For him, success also carries a sense of responsibility, especially in his role working with First Nations personnel in defence.

You need to make the right decisions. You can't really make too many wrong ones because it's not only the Elders watching you, but it's also the younger generation, they're also watching you.

Defining success on their own terms

The final pillar of success that emerged from conversations at Garma is wellbeing.

Sue-Anne Hunter, national commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people, says culture, language and connection to Country are central to the wellbeing and development of First Nations children and young people.

"Culture is the protective factor that keeps our children connected to their communities, to their families and to themselves," she tells SBS News.

Sue-Anne Hunter, national commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people, says the next generation has greater access to opportunities than ever before and is using its voice to influence the future. Source: Supplied / John Jiang

According to Hunter, young people today are accessing opportunities that were not available to many previous generations, while also using their voices to shape the future.

"What has changed is that this generation has more platforms, more opportunity and a voice they are willing to use, built on decades of advocacy by those who have come before them."

No young person should have to choose between who they are and where they are going.

Across conversations with young leaders at Gulkula, one message was clear: the future was not about choosing between where they wanted to go and where they came from — it was about carrying both forward.

title: Are you owed a share of $274 million in unclaimed money? Here's how to check
text:
In brief Services Australia says Australians are owed around $274 million in unclaimed Medicare benefits.

If you're owed, providing your bank details should allow you to receive the funds within days.

Hundreds of millions of dollars are waiting to be claimed by Australians who have not provided their current bank account details to Services Australia.

The agency says 974,000 Australians are owed a slice of $274.5 million in unpaid Medicare benefits.

It's urging people to check that their bank details are up to date in their Medicare online account.

The average amount owed per person is around $280.

Young Australians account for the largest share, with more than $65 million payable to 255,000 people aged between 18 and 24.

title: Why one tiny island's Census is about much more than numbers
text:
IN BRIEF Norfolk Island is an external territory of Australia and will take part in the Census on 11 August.

People can complete the Census online or on paper. Physical forms will be collected by field officers visiting Norfolk Island.

In the middle of the South Pacific Ocean, a tiny island spanning just 35 square kilometres will be included in this year's Census.

Home to about 2,100 residents, Norfolk Island has earned a reputation as "one of the most beautiful places on Earth", according to acting general manager of the Norfolk Island Regional Council (NIRC), Nicholas Mostardo.

He moved to the subtropical island early this year and says its natural beauty and close-knit community make it unlike anywhere else.

"It's got a rich environment, it's got very warm and kind people. It's probably one of the most unique places in the world that I've had personally the pleasure of being involved with," Mostardo told SBS News.

NIRC is currently under administration until 31 December 2026, as Norfolk Island transitions to what the Australian government has described as a "new bespoke governance model".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In the interim, Mostardo has been liaising with the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) to help ensure Norfolk Island's population is recorded during the Census of Population and Housing on 11 August.

"We've had several visits from the ABS zone manager and the assistant director of Census Mainstream and Enumeration. They've been coming out to ensure the community is well engaged and consulted on completing the form."

A decade in the making

The Census has been conducted in Australia for more than a century, but this will be the third time Norfolk Island has ever participated in the survey. It also marks a decade since the Australian government passed reforms that led to the island being included in the Census.

It's a change that was considered contentious by some.

In 1914, Norfolk became an Australian territory, but the "precise constitutional arrangement was not clear at the time", according to an online statement by legal advisory firm Norfolk Advisory.

Around 65 years later, the Australian parliament allowed Norfolk Islanders to form a limited self-government. Following governance reforms passed in 2015 and implemented in 2016, the Australian government assumed responsibility for the island's governance.

In 2023, Norfolk Island regained some involvement in its affairs through the establishment of a new advisory body, the Norfolk Island Governance Committee. The island is now considered an external territory of Australia.

This complex history has divided some people — including those of Pitcairn descent — about whether Norfolk Island should be counted during Australia's Census.

Pitcairn Islanders were a genetic mix of Tahitian and English, the English part being direct descendants from the mutineers on the HMS Bounty — a bloodline that still runs strong today. In 1856, 194 people arrived on Norfolk Island from the neighbouring Pitcairn Islands.

According to information shared with SBS News by Norfolk Island People for Democracy (NIPD), Pitcairn Islanders have a distinct culture and speak the Norf'k-Pitcairn language (also known as 'Pitkern-Norf'k' or 'Norfolk'), which blends 18th-century English and Tahitian.

NIPD has previously petitioned for the United Nations Special Committee on Decolonisation to recognise and list Norfolk Island as a non-self-governing territory. The group has described Australia's relationship with the island as a "bloodless genocide".

Norfolk Island ancestry

The ABS did not provide a statement to SBS News regarding Norfolk Island's participation in the Census. It did refer to online information available about how to complete the Census on Norfolk Island.

The ABS outlines that "ancestry data reported for Norfolk Island from the 2021 Census is not comparable with ancestry data reported from censuses prior to and including 2011". That's because of differences in the way the ancestry question was asked.

The 2011 Norfolk Island Census asked a specific question about whether a person was of Pitcairn descent. It reported that 38.4 per cent of the population identified as having Pitcairn descent.

READ MORE What is new in the 2026 Census? The questions that have changed

In Australia's 2016 Census, people could identify up to two responses when asked about their ancestry, with 29.6 per cent of usual residents indicating they had Pitcairn ancestry. During the 2021 Census, this decreased to 25.1 per cent.

The ABS notes that the number of people with Pitcairn ancestry increased from 484 in 2016 to 550 in 2021. This year, people can list up to four responses on the ancestry question.

Mostardo told SBS News that the ABS has made "some new arrangements" to provide a "better reflection of responses for people that live on Norfolk Island". He believes that has alleviated "some of the concerns that the community had [about the ancestry question] with prior censuses".

"The Census is important to Norfolk. You know, it really will assist us and the Commonwealth government with funding arrangements for the island; assisting with things like strategic planning and economic capacity as well," he said.

Norfolk Island was formed through volcanic activity in the Pacific Ocean and is located 1,676km northeast of Sydney. Credit: Peta McCartney

The Council of Elders, Norfolk Island — which serves as the elected leaders and custodians of traditional knowledge and expressions of culture on Norfolk Island — has posted content on social media regarding the Census.

In response to one Facebook user who questioned why Norfolk Island was included in the Australian Census, the group responded: "In 2016, when the ABS took over the Census, there were many shortfalls for Norfolk. The change made long-term planning for Norfolk difficult.

"As the Council of Elders' role is to advocate for the community, it became evident that we need to know more about the composition of our community today. The Council of Elders has engaged with the ABS to try to achieve this."

READ MORE Residents of a tiny Australian island are calling for a return to self-rule to save their culture

Households on Norfolk Island can complete the Census online or by using the paper form provided.

Paper forms can be returned to the Supper Room on the island during the morning from 10 August to 16 August. Otherwise, Census field officers will return to collect forms in the provided privacy envelope.

The ABS specified that forms should not be mailed back.

title: Why Australia could be heading for a spring and summer 'triple whammy'
text:
In brief Climate change, a strong El Niño and another climate driver could combine forces this spring.

However, there are signs it's not all bad news for the summer bushfire threat.

Three climate forces are lining up ahead of spring, raising the odds of hotter and drier weather across parts of Australia.

The world is facing a potentially record-breaking El Niño, with the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) forecasting it will continue to intensify into a "very strong event" that may persist well into next year.

At the same time, another Australian climate driver associated with warmer and drier conditions — a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) — is expected to develop by spring.

"So, for Australia through the coming spring and summer, the double whammy of climate change and El Niño will be driving our weather. In actual fact, we might even have a triple whammy," Andrew Watkins, an adjunct professor at Monash University and a Climate Council researcher, told SBS News.

He said the IOD "is effectively El Niño but in the Indian Ocean".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Unfortunately, that pattern really sets in until summer, when the Asian monsoon comes in and knocks it over. But if we have climate change and El Niño and a positive Indian Ocean dipole, they are three things that all push south-east Australia into hotter and drier, and especially the spring period," he said.

Will Australia see a repeat of Europe's summer?

While an El Niño does not necessarily mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia, it does raise the likelihood.

As parts of Europe and the United States swelter through a summer of scorching heatwaves and fires, BoM climatologist Zhi-Weng Chua says soon, much of Australia will likely swelter too.

He says there is a high chance much of the nation's south-east and south-west will experience one of the warmest springs on record.

"Western parts of Western Australia, extending into southern Queensland and parts of south Australia, there is a strong indication that temperatures will be in the top 20 per cent of historical records for spring," he told SBS News.

But the heat expected during Australia's spring and summer are driven by different factors to those pushing temperatures skyward in Europe and North America.

Those continents have experienced the impact of climate change in the past few months, with record-high temperatures leading to high fire danger.

READ MORE How is climate change affecting El Niño and La Niña?

El Niño is an event measured by the sea surface temperature of the Pacific Ocean — it has a strong impact on the Asia Pacific, but far less on Europe and North America.

Sea surface temperatures in the central Pacific are now more than 2C above average — a level associated with a very strong El Niño — for the first time in a decade.

Australia's bushfire outlook

Greg Mullins is the former commissioner of Fire and Rescue NSW.

In recent years, he has used his expertise to drive action on climate change preparedness and risk evaluation, as a member of the Climate Council.

He recently told SBS News this year's converging climate drivers were extremely worrying, noting that emergency agencies were working with the BoM ahead of the release of the spring bushfire seasonal outlook, which would help guide preparations.

He said the combination of an El Niño with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole could drive "flash droughts" that heighten bushfire risk.

"Those two together can drive rapid drought, what we call flash drought, that you know within weeks you're suddenly in bad fire territory," he said.

"I know there's a lot of deep concern in all the fire agencies nationally," he said.

However, BoM meteorologists said there are signs that rain could disrupt the summer bushfire threat in many areas.

"That drier than average pattern that we're seeing for September does break down for much of the country and we start seeing either above average rainfall being favoured or even a not-clear signal for a lot of the country," Chua said.

Victoria and Tasmania, however, are expected to remain comparatively dry, he said.

title: Two planes involved in near-miss while taxiing at Sydney Airport

Two planes have been involved in a near-miss while taxiing on the runway at Sydney Airport, forcing one plane to brake suddenly and injuring a crew member.

A Qatar Airways plane and a Jetstar plane were photographed on the runway metres from each other just after 7am on Sunday.

A Jetstar plane and a Qatar Airways plane on the runway at Sydney Airport on Sunday morning. Nine News

There were 180 passengers on board Jetstar flight JQ402, which was heading to the Gold Coast, when the pilot spotted a Qatar Boeing 777 aircraft next to the plane, Nine News reported. The Qatar plane did not have any passengers on board and was being towed at the time, according to the report.

The pilot applied the brakes on the Airbus A320, causing one flight attendant who was moving throughout the cabin to fall. The attendant was treated by paramedics for minor injuries. No passengers were injured.

Erone Fitzpatrick is a star – All-Australian, Carlton leader and selected in the Irish representative AFLW side – but there’s one thing about Australian rules football that leaves her baffled. Club loyalty – or rather, the lack of it. Hailing from County Laois in Ireland, Fitzpatrick helped lead them to their first Gaelic football title in over 20 years in 2022, before being poached by Carlton for the 2023 season. Carlton’s Erone Fitzpatrick will represent her homeland in the ALFW Aus vs Ireland clash. Joe Armao She played with the same teammates from age four to 23; switching clubs or counties is “unheard of at home”. “Talking to a lot of the Aussies here, they can’t get over how loyal you are to your club and your county throughout your whole career,” Fitzpatrick said. “I would play with the one club for my whole football career, and I would play with the one county for my whole football career, and they couldn’t get over that.

Advertisement

“That’s why we find it really strange, the whole trade period and people leaving clubs and going to different clubs and stuff like that.” Fitzpatrick hopes she can stick with her AFLW side in a similar way. “I would love that,” she said. “You never know what can happen in the future, but I think it would be very weird for me to go anywhere else. I think if you asked a lot of the Irish players, they would say the exact same thing.” Since the AFLW’s inaugural season in 2017, the presence of Gaelic football cross-coders has skyrocketed, with 44 active Irish players in the league and two inactive. Their effect has been profound. The Irish players play a lightning-fast and attacking style. North Melbourne, who have won two consecutive AFLW premierships, currently have five Irish players on their list, while the Brisbane Lions, Adelaide, Geelong and Carlton all have a strong contingent of Irish players. Erone Fitzpatrick is one of 46 Irish players in the AFLW. Joe Armao The impact in Ireland has been seismic as well. On one hand, the game’s popularity has surged, with Irish broadcasters showing AFLW games, dedicated 3am watch parties and growing fan bases on social media.

Advertisement

But the amount of Irish-born players lured to Australia has also left a growing hole in Gaelic football pathways, especially in smaller regions, “I’m from a very small county, not saying that I would have been a big fish, but I probably would have been at home,” Fitzpatrick explains. “For my county to lose like someone like me is hard ... because in a small county, talent is very limited compared to the bigger counties that have a huge pool of talent. “Counties like Mayo have six girls playing in the AFLW – that’s a huge chunk of unbelievable talent from one county.” There’s enough Irish talent in AFLW to make a representative game in the mould of State of Origin possible. Fitzpatrick represented Ireland in that match in Sydney, in front of a sellout crowd. Speaking in the lead-up, Fitzpatrick was thrilled to be part of it. Carlton star Erone Fitzpatrick was a pivotal part of the Blue’s surge into the prelim finals. AFL Photos

“My parents are flying out for the game, which is so important to me, and I’ll also have my aunties, family friends, my grannies’ next door neighbour,” she joked. “I want to make them proud, and I want to make all the young girls proud and know they can chase their dreams and be anything they want in life.” Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 ‘Faceless’ foes to face off as Carlton and St Kilda scrap for wildcard spot Now, the focus is on the upcoming AFLW season, which begins on Sunday at Marvel Stadium when Fitzpatrick’s Blues take on the Saints before the clubs’ men’s teams do the same. The Blues’ women’s side made it to a preliminary final last season, where they fell short against the Lions. It was a meteoric turnaround – Carlton finished 14th in 2024 before introducing a crop of young, extroverted talent in 2025. Fitzpatrick was a pivotal part of the resurgence last year, averaging 17.5 disposals and kicking 13 goals.

title: ‘They hid it away’: The DNA test that revealed an Australian cricketer’s family secret
text:
But the true significance of Gaunt’s debut has been shrouded in a family secret for decades, only recently confirmed by DNA testing: Ron Gaunt may well have been Australia’s first Test cricketer of Indigenous heritage.

After moving to Victoria, Gaunt also made his mark in the east, notably as the longtime bowling coach for the Footscray Cricket Club. It was there he set Merv Hughes on the path to a storied career by telling the young all-rounder from Werribee that he was, in fact, a bowler.

“He was quick and used to swing the ball about quite nicely. Especially on the Perth wicket where he used to get a bit of pace and bounce, he was a nasty proposition for a batsman to face. He was certainly a top-rate fast bowler,” Craig told Cricinfo in 2012.

Gaunt’s story was a good one, of a strapping quick bowler with a shock of red hair, who may well have played many more games for Australia had he not been stuck behind the likes of Alan Davidson and Graham McKenzie.

Within a few days, the 23-year-old Gaunt made his debut in Durban, claiming figures of 2-87 in a drawn match under the captaincy of Ian Craig.

In January 1958, a young West Australian fast bowler by the name of Ron Gaunt was flown into South Africa as an injury replacement for the Australian Test team.

Because of its rich wheat farming, York was home to plenty of prosperous families, who shared the land with the Indigenous community.

The municipality of York, about 100 kilometres east of Perth, is WA’s oldest inland town, established in 1831 after being home to the Ballardong Noongar people for thousands of years.

Gaunt’s story also raises a wider question of Australian cricket, and life. How many more gifted athletes of Indigenous heritage have been part of the nation’s story in secret, because of the past strictures of the White Australia policy?

Since then, Ash Gardner, Scott Boland and Brendan Doggett have joined the list of Indigenous Test cricketers. Boland will proudly take the field for Australia in a Test against Bangladesh in Darwin , amidst one of the nation’s largest Indigenous communities, this week.

His debut came a month earlier than the sole women’s Test played by Aunty Faith Thomas at Melbourne’s Junction Oval in February 1958, and decades before Jason Gillespie took the field for Australia in Sydney in 1996.

As the years went by, rumours circulated that the swarthy complexion of some children was down to Spanish ancestry, or even that someone in the family had married a Pacific Island princess. Anything but Indigenous heritage.

The secrecy started around the time of the First World War, when two family members served, including Arthur Gaunt. When he came back from Europe, Arthur listed his mother’s heritage as Maori, the better to receive a gratitude bond of £100 for returned servicemen.

“All this was kept a secret,” says Ron’s nephew, Dudley Gaunt. “There were laws and restrictions, and it just would’ve made their lives difficult. So they hid it away.”

Walter and Matilda raised her eldest son, Arthur, together, but also had other children, including another named Walter. After Walter junior grew up, he married Ruby Morse, and among six children Ron Gaunt was born in York in 1934.

Matilda Gaunt, who was Indigenous, is seated at right. She was Ron Gaunt’s grandmother.

Matilda was, by all accounts, a formidable figure. Local newspaper reports tell of how, aged 16, she took the local publican to court in York over unpaid wages and won the case. She was a landowner, and after having one child with another man, Matilda married Walter Gaunt, a local bricklayer.

In 1872, John Walkinshaw Cowan, whose brother would marry the revered social reformer and politician Edith Cowan, had a child with an unnamed Aboriginal woman. That child, Matilda Cowan, was Ron Gaunt’s grandmother.

“WA was a very harsh place for Aboriginal people,” says Ron’s niece, Jenny Ewell. “I think they wanted to avoid that, and absolutely because of Ron’s cricket.

It is ironic that two of Gaunt’s three Tests were played against Apartheid South African teams – just another reminder of the complexities facing a young man of mixed race in Australia in the 1950s and ’60s.

Gaunt was among the most promising young fast bowlers in the country, with enough of a competitive streak to indulge in a bit of “Bodyline” bowling for WA in 1956. In a game against Queensland, umpire Colley ordered WA captain Ken Meuleman to change the field, and warned Gaunt about his bowling.

When the Gaunt family moved from York to Perth, as Walter’s building business grew, he purchased land and built a house in a suburb called Rivervale, on the eastern bank of the Swan River. Tellingly, Rivervale was the nearest suburb on the outside of the prohibited area, which was only rescinded in 1954 – well after Ron had started playing club cricket.

In the west, a strict policy was introduced in 1927 to ban the Indigenous community from setting foot into the “Native Prohibited Area” that broadly covered the Perth central business district and select suburbs either side of the Swan River. And in Queensland, an Aboriginal fast bowler named Eddie Gilbert was swift enough to knock the bat out of Don Bradman’s hands, but not to play for Australia.

Much had changed in WA, and Australia, between the late 19th century and the 1930s. Intermarriage between whites and Aboriginal people was first discouraged, then virtually outlawed.

Gaunt, by this time nicknamed “Pappy”, would also mentor Tony Dodemaide, and was instrumental in helping the club win its inaugural first-grade premiership in 1980.

“What he did for me was extraordinary. Without him, I would’ve gone down to Footscray and battled away as a middle-order batsman and part-time bowler. If I had said to Ron, ‘You’re kidding yourself, I’m a batsman’, I’d probably still be plugging away in Footscray thirds now...”

“I reckon I bowled three balls and Ron came down and said you don’t bat any more, you’re a bowler. He stood at the top of my mark for two or three years, just talking bowling, theories, sorting batsmen out, a whole gamut of different things.

“I was a middle-order batsman who bowled maybe second or third change and then got down to Footscray and had a talk to the president, the coach, Ken Eastwood was in on the conversation as seconds captain, and Ron Gaunt was there,” Hughes says.

“Ron absolutely loved playing cricket, he lived and breathed the game, and I think it would have just destroyed him had he not been able to play it. So that’s probably where it came from.”

Hughes remembers Gaunt’s skill as a technical coach, plus his ability to still send down beautiful outswing in the nets. But what sticks with him is the older man’s personal touch – sports psychology before it had the name.

“You could talk to him about anything,” Hughes says. “He could pick up on if you were having a bad day or whatever, and that’s the philosophy I take with kids now. You talk to them, and it’s not just about cricket, but about school, are exams coming up? If guys aren’t concentrating on their bowling, you try to get to the bottom of it, and he used to do that beautifully.

”He knew you had the talent and if you weren’t producing at training he’d try to get to the bottom of it. He’d say, ‘Listen, you’re at training, you can leave that behind, and concentrate on your training’.”

Merv Hughes was mentored by Ron Gaunt at Footscray. Getty

Some earthier incentives came when Hughes and Footscray were fighting for their lives in the 1980 first-grade grand final.

“In the first XI grand final I played in my second year at Footscray, there was 10 and 11 batting, and he just said, ‘Right boys, if you can get to double figures here I’ll buy you a slab’,” Hughes remembers. “How hard do you reckon we worked to get those runs?

“If you did well, he was always there for you. It wasn’t him beating his chest, it was just him patting you on the back and saying, ’Well done’.”

Dodemaide, a couple of years younger than Hughes, can recall watching Gaunt bowl, perhaps planting a seed that led an initially front-on bowler to change his action to allow for the away swingers that netted Dodemaide 10 Test caps.

Australian selector Tony Dodemaide (right). Getty Images

“He had the tracksuit on and was clearly well past playing age, but he went in to bowl a few balls and demonstrate what he was talking about, and he had this beautiful side-on jump and action, and it was just so smooth,” says Dodemaide, now an Australian selector. “I thought, ‘Wow, could I ever bowl like this bloke?’

“Having a couple of Test players around the club was just gold for a young kid like me. He only played a handful of Tests, but that was enough as far as we were concerned – to spend any time around someone who’d played at that level of cricket.”

None of Hughes, Dodemaide or even his fellow Footscray Test cricketer Ken Eastwoood had any idea about Gaunt’s heritage.

“I never knew that, but that’s a real feather in his cap,” Hughes says. “Times have changed for the better. I thought I spent a fair bit of time with him, but it was never mentioned. Back then he might’ve been hiding that heritage.”

There is one former teammate, Lindsay James, who has told Dodemaide that Gaunt did indeed know of his Indigenous heritage, and that the pair discussed it quietly, once, long after both had finished playing and coaching.

“I couldn’t imagine him being a fearsome fast bowler,” Dodemaide says. “He had such a gentle demeanour about him, and very generous with his time and experience.”

After retirement, Gaunt moved to the NSW Central Coast to share more time with his children, Karon and Andrew. Gaunt and their mother had divorced when Andrew was two years old.

“Once a year we used to get to see my father around Christmas time for a month, [and] then he’d have to go back to Victoria to work,” Andrew says. “But when I was around 21-22, I went and stayed with him for a few years, and that was good. He was pretty much just like a mate, he spoke like a mate and that’s how we were.

“I came back to Sydney after a couple of years, and we kept in closer contact, and, eventually, he retired up the Central Coast and I went up and stayed there for a while. But work was back here in Sydney. So I was always going up there weekly, pretty much for years.”

Australian Test players Ron Gaunt (left) who played his first Test against South Africa with captain Bob Simpson and Richie Benaud. "The News" and "The Mail"

Sport in general, and cricket in particular, was never far away from the conversation.

“You had no choice on the TV, it was cricket when it started until it finished, then he’d go, ‘OK it’s yours now’,” Andrew recalls. “He never boasted, he never bragged, that wasn’t him. Other people who knew him would say, ‘That’s Ronnie Gaunt, he used to play for Australia’. But he’d never say that. He wouldn’t talk too much about it – what happens on tour stays on tour almost.”

If Gaunt was taciturn about his cricket achievements, his heritage was buried deeper still, remaining unknown to the family when Ron died in 2012. Eight years later, during COVID-19, Andrew’s half-sister Kellie started digging into family history. Ancestry searches were followed by DNA tests, revealing a hidden Indigenous bloodline.

Indigenous Test star Scott Boland. Getty Images

“One day, out of the blue she gave me a call and said, ‘Andrew, guess what, you’ll never believe it’, and I just said, ‘Nah, get out of here’. And my other sister Karon couldn’t believe it at all.

“Then Kellie got in contact with Jenny, and she took it up and ran with it. It was a such a well-kept secret, and maybe that was a reason why. He may not have played for Australia or got the chances he did if they knew he had Indigenous background.

“I was speaking to my sisters about Jason Gillespie saying, ‘Geez, he’s supposed to be the first person of Indigenous blood to play for Australia’. I started laughing about that and going, ‘Oh man, sorry about that’.”

Ask Andrew what he might have said to his father had he known, and he pauses.

“I’d probably have said, ‘What the hell were you thinking?’” he laughs. “I’m actually quite proud or glad, it just cements that footprint in our family as a full-on Aussie. But I don’t think they looked at it like that.”

While Ron got his mother Ruby’s red hair, Andrew and Jenny are both darker in complexion. Andrew can remember, as a teenager, that Ron got them together at Martin Place in Sydney.

“I met Jenny one time when I was about 16,” he says. “Dad was in Melbourne at the time, but he came up to see us. He wanted me to go and meet my cousin, he goes, ‘Come and meet your cousin’, and Karon said, ‘What about me?’ and he says, ‘Nah, just Andrew’. I thought that was a bit odd.

“That’s the first and last time I met Jenny [who moved to the United States, where she still lives]. But I think Dad was sizing me up with her because we were both darker in complexion. That’s just my take, but my sisters Karon and Kellie thought that made sense.”

After Jenny took up the family research, she passed much of the information onto Dudley Gaunt, who still lives in WA. He has had inconclusive discussions with WA Cricket about Ron’s Indigenous heritage, and has also made attempts to contact the Ballardong Noongar community. Cricket Australia is looking into the Gaunt family story.

“We want to ensure cricket’s heritage fully reflects all those from different backgrounds who have contributed to the game,” a CA spokesman said.

“The stories provided by those exploring family ancestry is an important way to ensure the diverse backgrounds of past players is recognised.”

Dudley says the main issue in his meeting with WA Cricket was not Gaunt’s Aboriginality, “It was whether he accepted his Aboriginality, whether he told people. Did he tell people at South Perth cricket club?

“If he wouldn’t have been able to play cricket, why would he tell anyone at South Perth that he was Aboriginal? It was a different time, they parked it away, hid it and got on with their lives.”

In 2005, the former chief justice of NSW, James Spiegelman, spoke about hidden Aboriginal histories in that year’s Charles Perkins Oration.

“Let me state one undeniable fact: many, probably millions of Australians have an Aboriginal ancestor,” he said. “This should be recognised as an important bond. However, most do not know this fact about their family.

“There was a strong sense of racism involved in the suppression in thousands upon thousands of Australian families of the Aboriginal origins of one or more of their forebears. For most of our history this has been regarded as a matter to be suppressed.

“It appears to me that the process of reconciliation would be advanced by a wider recognition across the broad Australian community that the number of Australians who have Aboriginal ancestors probably amounts to millions.

“The reconciliation process cannot succeed if it is based, contrary to historical fact, solely on maintaining a rigid and categorical distinction between black and white. It will succeed if a significant proportion of those Australians of whom it is true take pride in acknowledging their roots in both communities.”

For Jenny, the secret is itself a significant part of the story.

“I was very proud to find that out myself, to think we’ve got heritage that goes back 60,000 years in Australia,” she says. “But in going back to speak to the family, I found out that the family did know, and didn’t say anything.

“I was shocked, thinking, ‘Gosh they kept it a good secret all those years’. But a lot of it might have been that they wanted to work and get on with their lives. This is my opinion – because Ron was playing cricket and very successful, they wanted that to keep going and that it wasn’t made more difficult for him.”

Andrew recalls one other comment from his father that has taken on new meaning.

“My dad used to tell me, ‘You have a whole other family in the west’,” he says. “It was a big secret, and back then I could understand it. Whereas now I’m like, ‘Wow, that’s cool’.”

title: How an Australian mining company was caught in Trump’s tightening Cuba noose
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations How an Australian mining company was caught in Trump’s tightening Cuba noose Michael Koziol August 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On the outskirts of a city called Moa, at the south-eastern end of Cuba, flies a Canadian flag. Its maple leaf flaps proudly beside the red triangle and white star of Cuba’s own national banner. The flags mark the Moa Nickel mine, a joint venture between Canadian mining company Sherritt International and Cuban state-owned La Compania General de Niquel. Ore is extracted, shipped to Alberta in Canada and refined into nickel and cobalt. The Canadian flag flies next to the Cuban flag at the Moa Joint Venture, a nickel mine in southeastern Cuba. Google Maps In May, as part of efforts to crush Cuba’s communist regime, the Trump administration imposed sanctions on Moa Nickel. The mine, already hit by fuel shortages after the US choked off Cuba’s Venezuelan lifeline, has shut down – as has Sherritt’s refinery in Fort Saskatchewan, Canada. Now, the Trump administration is doing the same thing to a fledgling gold and copper mine part-owned by an Australian company, Antilles Gold. And in both cases, the solution appears to be the same: sell a stake to the Americans, possibly to friends of US President Donald Trump.

Advertisement

“Their choices are to leave, stay and then have an immense amount of problems, or try to find a saviour,” said John Kavulich, president of the US-Cuba Trade and Economic Council, a New York-based business network. “If I’m an executive of Antilles Gold in Australia, I’m waiting for someone to stick a gun in my stomach. Thus far, that’s the only thing the Trump administration hasn’t done.” ASX-listed Antilles Gold was slapped with US sanctions in early June when its Cuban joint venture, Minera La Victoria, was blacklisted. The company, which is headquartered at an unassuming home in the NSW town of Bowral, owns 50 per cent of the venture through its Cayman Islands-registered subsidiary, Antilles Gold Inc. Its main project is the Nueva Sabana open-pit copper and gold mine in central Cuba, 25 kilometres south-east of Ciego De Avila. According to Antilles’ ASX filings, the earthworks, water supply and site preparation began in early December, and a Chinese company, Xinhua Mining, was given the go-ahead on a $US30 million ($42 million) engineering and construction contract on New Year’s Eve.

Advertisement

Antilles Gold says work has halted while it scrambles to deal with the impact of June’s sanctions. It says the company has submitted a proposal to the US State Department that would involve selling at least 51 per cent of shares in the Caymans-based subsidiary to an acceptable US investor. Who might that be? The company’s chairman, Brian Johnson, won’t say. Neither will Kavulich, who has been working with Antilles Gold. “I can’t go there,” he said. The Moa Nickel mine in Cuba, a joint venture between Canada’s Sherritt International and a state-owned enterprise. Google In the case of Canada’s Sherritt International, its potential saviour is an entity called Gillon Capital – the family office of Heather and Ray Washburne, who happens to be a close ally of Trump. The companies are in exclusive negotiations for Gillon to take a 55 per cent stake in Sherritt at a discount to its closing value on May 15 (it had already crashed from $US0.25 a share to $US0.09 following the US sanctions).

Advertisement

The State Department and US Treasury cleared the way for the talks to take place, but will need to approve any final deal. Washburne is a businessman, investor and real estate developer who co-founded a restaurant chain in Texas. A long-time Republican donor, in 2016 he was described by the Texas Tribune as “Trump’s most visible fundraiser” in Dallas. Ray Washburne, pictured in 2018, was a major fundraiser for Donald Trump in Texas, and was appointed by him to run the Overseas Private Investment Corporation. Getty Images for Concordia Summit In his first term, Trump appointed Washburne to run the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, the federal government’s development bank, and he later served on Trump’s intelligence advisory board. He no longer holds either position. Sherritt’s initial response to the expanded US sanctions was to say it would relinquish its stake in the Cuban venture, which it built over 30 years. But that changed. Bloomberg News reported that Sherritt’s interim chief executive, Peter Hancock, was at home in Canada watching cycling when Washburne called him to make the offer.

Advertisement

“This deal happened because an actor in the United States was able to make a case to the US State Department,” Hancock told Bloomberg. “We were collateral damage in a larger policy objective for the United States.” Washburne doesn’t see it that way at all. Reached by phone on Thursday (US time), he said he was rescuing Sherritt and its mine from certain ruin, and the Trump administration had nothing to do with arranging the deal. US President Donald Trump boards Air Force One on Friday. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson “The company was in severe financial straits to begin. I’ve known about the company for years, I’ve followed it, I knew that it had some valuable assets to it,” he told this masthead. “When I saw the sanctions were put in place – I didn’t have any idea they were doing that – I just called the company and said: do you need capital? If I hadn’t come in, it would have already been shut down and gone.”

Advertisement

Gillon Capital was spun out of an existing family office, A. G. Hill Partners, linked to the Hunt family dynasty. Washburne’s wife Heather, née Hill, is a descendant of Texas oil tycoon Haroldson Lafayette Hunt Jr, who secured the rights over much of the enormous East Texas Oil Field. Related Article Explainer

Trump diplomacy ‘Cuba is finished’: What does Trump want with the island nation? Gillon does not own any other mining interests at present, although the family – through oil heirs Nelson and William Hunt – once owned part of one of the world’s largest silver mines, in Idaho. Washburne says he cold-called Sherritt himself when he saw the Canadian miner was in trouble. “I literally just found the guy’s phone number … It had nothing to do at all with the administration. I had no discussion with them at all.” He said he was not aware of Australian company Antilles Gold and its Cuba venture, and was not in discussions with them. But he was interested, and asked for their contact details. Washburne’s late mother was Australian, born in Sydney between the wars.

Advertisement

Antilles Gold chairman Johnson told this masthead that the company had identified a suitable American investor, and it was not Gillon Capital, although he would not disclose who it was. The firm’s proposal to the State Department remained confidential, he said. The Australian government confirmed it had engaged with Antilles Gold and US officials on the matter, but would not answer questions about those discussions. The State Department did not respond to inquiries. Cuba’s former president Raul Castro, 94, arrives at a gathering for International Workers’ Day in Havana on May 1, 2026. AP John Kirk, a professor emeritus of Latin American studies at Dalhousie University in Nova Scotia, Canada, said it was noteworthy that the State Department appeared to have no objection to Gillon Capital taking over the mine in Cuba. “Clearly, Trump is supporting his friends in the stealthy takeover of Cuban commerce,” Kirk said. “I suspect that a similar path will be found for Antilles Gold. In both cases, greed, hypocrisy and bullying have been implemented by the Trump administration.”

Advertisement

ASIC records show Antilles Gold was first registered in South Australia in 1984 as Aytox Pty Ltd. It has been through several name changes; as EnviroGold and Panterra Gold, it developed a mine in the Dominican Republic in the 2010s. The company had been turning its attention to a second Cuban project, a planned gold, silver and antimony mine on the Isla de la Juventud (the Isle of Youth). Infill drilling was supposed to start at the La Demajagua mining concession in the second half of this year, until the sanctions hit. A man pulls a cart carrying drinking water during a power outage in Havana, Cuba, last week. AP Photo/Ramon Espinosa For foreign firms, the main effect of US sanctions is on banking. Any company using US dollars is likely to be cut off by a financial institution. Even if there’s doubt, banks are generally risk-averse and won’t want to take the chance, Kavulich says. The US continues to impose new sanctions on Cuba and its interests. On Thursday, it designated a number of entities and people related to the procurement and sustainment of Cuban weapons.

Advertisement

“They went after the Cuban companies and ministries that everyone knows about first,” Kavulich says. “Now, they’re going granular, and they’re going deeper and deeper and deeper.” Related Article Updated

Cuba US brings criminal charges against former Cuban president Raul Castro Asked whether he thought the Trump administration’s approach to foreign companies operating in Cuba was effectively a shakedown, he said: “One person’s shakedown is another person’s benevolent opportunity to do what’s right.” Last month, the State Department released a 100-page report on the dangers Cuban communism posed to America and the Western world. Havana was “a staging ground where the ambitions of Moscow, Beijing, and Tehran converge with the radical movements operating inside our own borders”, it concluded, referring to the far-left. The report frames Cuba as a major security threat, thereby laying the groundwork for potential military intervention, which has been the subject of much speculation over the past six months. Meanwhile, it keeps tightening the noose on the country’s collapsed economy.

Advertisement

“They certainly can’t wait us out,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told US news site Axios. “Every time they create a new mechanism in which they try to get out of the noose, we just close it off.” Emily Morris, an economist and researcher specialising in Cuba at University College London, said the administration’s endgame was not clear, but “if any deal were done, it could well be a deal that allows US businesses in [to Cuba] but not others”. Paolo Spadoni, an associate professor at Augusta University and a recognised Cuba expert, said the primary motivation of Trump’s intervention was political, rather than a play for resources. “I think what he wants is to achieve what other presidents for many decades have not been able to achieve,” he said. “And there are economic benefits down the road.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world. title: Inflation numbers to bring relief for mortgage holders
text:
Mortgage holders will likely be able to breathe a sigh of relief with the Reserve Bank largely tipped to keep interest rates on hold.

Governor Michele Bullock and the central bank's board will meet on Monday and Tuesday, with economists forecasting the cash rate to stay at 4.35 per cent.

The prediction follows a surprise fall in inflation, despite it still being well above the bank's target band of two to three per cent.

Michele Bullock will preside over Reserve Bank board meetings on Monday and Tuesday. (Dean Lewins/AAP PHOTOS)

June data revealed headline inflation fell from four to 3.8 per cent for the month, the lowest levels since the start of the Iran war.

Trimmed mean inflation, the RBA's preferred measure, remained steady at 3.6 per cent.

Senior economist at NAB, Taylor Nugent, said the RBA would likely fall into line with market forecasts.

"The RBA would need a push to deliver further tightening and the net of data flow since May has not given them that push," he said.

"Unemployment is a little above their forecast and underlying inflation marginally lower than feared."

Mr Nugent said the RBA would likely monitor the impact of higher fuel prices on inflation following the removal of the federal government's fuel excise discount and oil prices spiking due to renewed volatility in the Middle East.

"NAB expects the next move (by the RBA) will ultimately be down but inflation risks do remain elevated," he said.

HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham said the central bank would likely take a wait-and-see approach before choosing to make a move on the cash rate.

The RBA will likely monitor the impact of higher fuel prices following the fuel excise discount. (Joel Carrett/AAP PHOTOS)

"That being said, as inflation is still above target, we expect the central bank to continue to express concern that inflation is too high," he said.

"We see the downswing in growth being sufficient that the RBA begins to cut its cash rate in H2 2027."

Mr Bloxham said there was still a chance, if inflation does not fall fast enough, that the RBA could still lift rates later in 2026.

"With trimmed mean inflation now having been above the mid-point of the RBA's target band for over four years, we see the board's tolerance for upside surprises or a slower-than-currently-projected return of inflation to target, as likely to be low."

Ms Bullock will also face a parliamentary inquiry on Friday, where the bank's board will come under scrutiny.

Tuesday will also have fresh figures on business confidence be released when NAB's latest monthly survey is unveiled.

Wall Street is meanwhile on the advance, with the US economy unexpectedly shedding jobs and amid dampened expectations the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose on Friday 151.83 points, or 0.28 per cent, to 54,036.93, the S&P 500 gained 0.62 per cent, to 7,757.64 and the Nasdaq 1.30 per cent, to 26,690.62.

title: Premier pens deal with ChatGPT developer on US trip
text:
The premier who led Australia's world-first social media ban has signed a landmark artificial intelligence agreement as he courts big tech.

While touring the US, South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas visited OpenAI's headquarters in San Francisco where he signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with its co-founder and president Greg Brockman.

OpenAI is the developer of ChatGPT, the world's most popular generative AI chatbot.

South Australia will explore artificial intelligence opportunities with ChatGPT's developer. (Mick Tsikas/AAP PHOTOS)

It is believed to be the first time an Australian state or territory government has inked an MoU with a major AI company.

The agreement will provide opportunities to develop AI skills, accelerate local research and innovation, attract global investment and spread the benefits of AI across South Australia, Mr Malinauskas said.

"We want to lead with ambition and care," he said in a statement on Sunday.

"Any initiative taken forward will be human-led and subject to the legal, privacy, security and procurement safeguards South Australians expect."

The federal government in April announced an MoU with Anthropic, creator of the Claude AI assistant.

State leaders are set to meet with the prime minister to discuss uniform standards for data centres. (George Chan/AAP PHOTOS)

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has since flagged plans to introduce legal requirements governing AI use and data centres.

He will convene a meeting of the nation's leaders later in August to discuss data centres and reach agreement on uniform standards.

Six states have agreed to the framework but Queensland and the Northern Territory are holding out.

Mr Malinauskas has been rubbing shoulders with US lawmakers, defence officials and tech leaders during a trade and investment mission, visiting New York, Washington DC, Maryland, Virginia and California so far.

I want to ensure the government is doing everything it can to make sure artificial intelligence delivers real benefits for people.

The premier, who got the ball rolling on Australia's move to restrict children younger than 16 from accessing social media, spoke about the ban during a meeting with Apple's outgoing chief executive Tim Cook.

Advertisement Advertisement

"To its great credit, Apple is rolling out stronger parental controls on its devices soon, giving parents greater control over how their children use devices such as iPhones and iPads," Mr Malinauskas wrote in a post on social media.

"Mr Cook has made clear that these changes have been inspired in part by the Australian social media age limit.

"We also had an important discussion about artificial intelligence and what the future of the technology could mean for our economy and society."

Mr Malinauskas is expected to return to Australia on Friday.

title: Caravan family's dream life backfires after drastic move: 'Wasn't working'
text:
Daniel and Apryl Oliver had spent years dreaming about travelling around Australia, but like many families, life kept getting in the way.

They had a home, two young daughters, Charlotte and Lillie, and a love for camping, but weekends and annual leave never felt like enough time together.

After moving to Muswellbrook in the NSW Hunter Valley so Daniel could work in the mines and create a better lifestyle for the family, they quickly realised the plan had backfired.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The goal was simple — more money, more time back, better family-work balance," the couple told Yahoo News.

"We did that for about two years. We rented our old house out, had to refinance, and the tenants' situation wasn't working the way we'd hoped. Interest rates kept climbing.

"We'd lost the family time we'd actually moved for."

The Oliver family have spent more than two years exploring Australia while homeschooling their daughters on the road. Source: Instagram/aussiesfindingourway

A new definition of success

With rising costs and a mortgage, Apryl was working two jobs and Daniel was spending long hours away at work. The couple decided it was time for a major change.

They sold their home, bought a caravan, cleared their debts, set off with their two daughters, and aimed to travel for 12 to 18 months.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

More than two years later, they're still exploring Australia and say the decision has completely changed how they view success.

"My definition of success now is memories over things," they said.

"We used to dream about the big house, full of furniture, two cars — all of it. Now we're minimalists. Everything we need fits in a caravan.

"As long as we're happy as a family, that's success."

Homeschooling on the road

The Oliver family, known for their social media account Aussies Finding Our Way, have travelled thousands of kilometres across Australia while also homeschooling their daughters on the road.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Daniel and Apryl said education has become a completely different experience for Charlotte, 7, and Lillie, 4, with everyday adventures becoming part of their learning.

"We believe our girls are learning more from this lifestyle — seeing things, going places, hands-on real-life skills — than they would sitting in a classroom," they said.

"It's a different set of lessons, but as parents do this, our kids are learning what we believe is right, not just what the schooling system says is right.

"We were worried our girls would miss out, but honestly, I'd say they've grown more out here than they would have staying in one town seeing the same faces every day."

Chasing the dream

The Oliver family has had to adapt to living in a much smaller space, manage limited power and water, find campsites, and deal with unexpected repairs.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"Online you see the sunrises, the sunsets, all the good stuff — but there's so much going on behind the scenes that never makes it into a photo," they said.

The couple said one of the biggest surprises has been watching their daughters build friendships and confidence while travelling.

RELATED

The family swapped their four-bedroom home for a caravan after deciding to chase a different kind of life on the road. Source: Instagram/aussiesfindingourway

The family wants other Aussies dreaming of a similar lifestyle to know it doesn't require a huge budget or a luxury set-up.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Their advice is simple: Stop waiting for the perfect time.

"We didn't want to die wondering 'what if'," they said.

"Our take is — you only get one shot at life. Even if it doesn't work out, at least you gave it a real go.

"There'll always be another house, another situation if things don't pan out.

"But you could also open your eyes to a completely different life, if you just let go and chase what you actually want."
